subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 36 to present a
petition signed by several petitioners from southwestern Ontario who call upon Parliament to reject the current proposal for a goods and services tax, to reform the taxation system so that there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations, ensure that if and when there is a broad public consensus on a sales tax measure to replace the manufacturers' sales tax this reform not be an opportunity for the government to impose a massive tax grab, and cause the government to cease with a proposal which will shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reform.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege for me to have this opportunity pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present a number of petitions from people from Brocklehurst, North Kamloops, Westsyde, Heffley Creek, Raleigh, Aberdeen, Valleyview and Dallas, British Columbia, who are all concerned about the government's goods and services tax.
Quite frankly, they cannot understand why the government would proceed with a tax that will tax reading material. It will make Canada the only country in the world that is actually imposing a tax on books, magazines, newspapers and reading material, which helps young people develop their reading and communication skills, to say nothing about their education generally.
These petitioners are saying that the government should stop proceeding with this tax, go back to the drawing-board and start all over again with real tax reform.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary who, as we all know, is a very knowledgeable person in terms of the bill. He has been here for several years and he also knows procedure.
In the motion put by the government, the third paragraph states that the message from the Senate in regard to amendment 5(b) will be accepted by the

government and proceeded with. In her remarks yesterday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration stated, as reported at page 11061 of Hansard:
The Senate had asked us in recommendation 5(b) to reduce this-
-that is, the penalty provisions-
- to two years and we agreed to this recommendation. We did not agree to it in the previous message because it will have some impact on our ability to fund the Labour Force Development Strategy. I would remind members that every dollar we take off the one side is not available for the other side. But we do recognize the value of compromise and we are committed to some very fundamental principles, but we are not intransigent. For that reason we are going to accept this recommendation.
At the end of the minister's speech, Madam Speaker, as you know, she tabled a motion which is lengthy and which I will not read. In it, she makes the claim that the government, conscious of this fellowship with its predecessors, reaffirms its sole and undoubted democratic right which will not in this manner be waived. Yet, prior to making the motion, she did waive the privileges of the House of Commons and reaffirmed again that there is some confusion in the government's thinking.
I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary this. How can this House adopt a motion that says that we will not waive our democratic right, our sole and undoubted rights, our privilege of being the sole House that imposes charges upon the state, and accept that the minister did exactly that? By her own admission yesterday, the minister said that this will cost the Government of Canada money.
There is in my view a double standard here. What is the Parliamentary Secretary's answer to this predicament? We have the acceptance of a money amendment made by the Senate which, in the words of the minister and previous speakers in this debate, was not to be accepted by the House. Yet, we have the government accepting it. How can he reconcile that? I would like to have an answer to that.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased and honoured to rise again in the House to discuss Bill C-21 and the recommended amendments as proposed by the other place, about which we have heard so much.
I find it unbelievable that the government has chosen this time to inflict more hardships on Canadians, when they are faced with such high interest rates, the proposed GST, and a faltering economy. As has been stated by many speakers in this House on this topic, Canadians, and especially my constituents, are not fooled into thinking that this is a good bill.
Bill C-21 is a further attack on the working people throughout this country. It is an attack on those communities that lack industry and depend on seasonal employment, an attack on the underdeveloped areas and an attack on the basic foundations of our country.
At the same time that this bill is being proposed, the government is trying to turn the tables by placing the blame on the victims, those people who depend on seasonal employment and therefore on unemployment insurance to meet life's basic needs.
The hon. member across the floor was very quick to blame the people of Atlantic Canada for using UI as a form of social welfare. We all know that this is not the case. As I stated a few moments ago, the Atlantic region is not a heavily industrialized area and seasonal employment is the way of life, not by choice but by economic necessity.
The implication in all of this is that those who are not working 12 months a year are somehow trying to beat the system. What makes this attitude so ridiculous is that it comes at a time when federal fiscal policy is increasing our number of unemployed in its so-called battle against inflation.
A 10 to 12 week job with varying hours is not the preferred employment of the people of Prince Edward Island. What I must stress here is that it is the only employment. It is not their fault. It is simply an economic reality, the reality of living in an economically underprivileged and neglected part of Canada. Toughening the
entrance requirements and shortening the benefit periods will impose further hardships on my province, on Atlantic Canada and on those people who are already living on the economic brink. Combined with the severe economic hardships associated with seasonal employment, the UI changes constitute a double hardship with very far-reaching effects on those who are seasonally employed and in turn on their families.
I would like to quote the Minister of Labour for Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Roberta Hubley: "Approximately 1,700 claimants on Prince Edward Island will no longer be able to establish a claim as a result of changes to unemployment insurance entrance requirements. Prince Edward Island recorded the largest percentage of claimants affected by entrance requirement changes. Prince Edward Island recorded the third largest percentage of claimants affected by changes to the UI benefit duration". She further stated that approximately 7,000 claimants in P.E.I. will be affected by changes to the UI benefit duration. Prince Edward Island has been singled out to bear more than its fair share of the cost of the proposed UI changes, particularly in relation to new entrance requirements. These changes will mean an increase in the absolute number of welfare recipients and will be a major blow to many residents of Prince Edward Island.
Since this bill was first introduced, I have listened to various groups, special committees and many of my constituents, and the majority of the views expressed fear of Bill C-21. The major fear is of welfare and unemployment.
Quite often the argument used by hon. members across the way is the same old song and dance about the other place. According to them, it should not even examine this bill, or if it must examine it, should ignore the wishes expressed by the people of Canada. According to the people across the floor, it should silence its conscience and without saying a word rubber stamp this legislation. I totally disagree.
The other place serves a very useful purpose. The government is not listening to the people. It is doing exactly as it wants because of its majority and that is not what democracy is about. It is true, and I would be the first to admit this, the government did win a majority. They won the majority due, in large part, to a wonderful advertising campaign. However, I would like to stress that we have checks and balances in this system. One of
May 8, 1990

the roles of the other place is to be one of these checks and balances.
However, the government has to listen. That is why we have an opposition, another Chamber and, in this particular House we have three parties. All the members of this House represent all of the people of Canada.
We often hear about the number of Canadian citizens who live below the poverty line. Those Canadians must depend on food banks in order to survive. It is not a very nice fact that 3.7 million of our country's citizens live below the poverty line, but even more shocking is the fact that a quarter of these are children under the age of 16. Furthermore, one in six Canadian children is undernourished. This is a fact. As Winnipeg sociologist, Harvey Stein, stated, "Poverty, you see, is not a vote getter. The people who use food banks are certainly not the folks who make a difference at election time."
It is very sad and it is also very true. The poor, whether they be working or unemployed, are obviously not the people that politicians seem so often obsessed with when an election or hand-outs are coming. They never consider the public welfare or the fate of the underprivileged.
Senator Jacques Hebert said: "This is the only explanation that comes to mind when I try to understand why the government had the audacity to introduce a bill like C-21, which will increase the suffering of the poor and cruelly affect the many people who already face hunger."
What I find very scary about the whole situation is that, with the increase in unemployment, the cut-back in benefits and the heavy burden placed on our welfare system, what we will have are more underprivileged, undernourished and underutilized Canadians and this is a very sad situation. In Atlantic Canada it is even more sad, because we have the highest unemployment rate and the highest welfare levels. Quite often we hear the Minister of Employment and Immigration boasting about retraining and job creation and about the way this is going to solve all of our problems. Certainly we need training, and we need qualified people all over the country to do the training. In many instances, the bottom line is that you can do all the training you want, but in
Government Orders
certain areas there are not very many jobs where these people can work.
In my home province of Prince Edward Island, and all over Atlantic Canada, the number of jobs for which you can retrain people is very limited. We realize that we can train people, who then could move on to other parts of Canada or to other areas of their region. There is nothing wrong with this, but when you train people with money taken from unemployed people for jobs that do not exist, it does not seem like a very realistic goal.
I suggest that the government, with all its great ideas and its many millions of dollars, should create an economic and industrial situation where realistic industries will be established in the outlying parts of the country. This will give people a place to work, where they can be trained for jobs. They can then go on from there.
I agree with a statement that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace has made on many occasions, that the training money should not come from the pockets of those who pay unemployment insurance premiums, neither the employer nor the employees.
Many people say: "There are lots of jobs in central Canada. What is wrong with young people moving to find work?" There is nothing wrong with that. In fact, it is good for young people to move around their country. Many people have moved from east to central Canada and to the west. People from the west have moved to central Canada and to the east. This is a great thing.
It is very easy for us to say this, but there are many people in the age group 30 to 40 who are already married and raising families. It is very hard for them to uproot themselves and move to other parts of the country, when they do not know whether jobs exist there. It does not matter where many of these people live, they do not want to leave that particular part of the country, because neither their parents nor grandparents left it.
The cold hard facts of life may be that this is what is going to come, and that we have to prepare people in a different way. There has to be another way of teaching people that perhaps the part of the country where they grew up is not where they will be able to live. This is a very cruel thing to say.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
In conclusion, if the government's true goal is positive reform of unemployment insurance, it should not hesitate to pass any of the amendments that are proposed by the other place. The amendments are moderate, sensible and sensitive to both the government's professed goal of deficit reduction, and the needs and dignity of unemployed Canadians.
The key word is dignity. For this reason, I fully support these amendments and urge the government opposite to do the same.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today, I will again try to convince all Canadian parliamentarians of the relevance of Bill C-21, tabled by our government to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. I will look at this reform from the perspective of the twenty-first century. I will then consider the political aspects of the new legislation and its positive impact on the labour force across this country.
As you know, the text of this legislation reflects the goals of our comprehensive Labour Force Development Strategy, and in fact, both documents form a whole. Our objective is to get employers, unions, governments and all Canadians involved in taking every initiative they consider appropriate to raise the level of skills of our workers.
We also want to implement the policies, programs and employment approaches that will help workers achieve their potential in a technological world where the demand for skills is becoming increasingly sophisticated. The government intends, without further delay, to take appropriate steps to ensure that Canada's labour force is able to adjust to rapid changes in the job environment as a result of major demographic shifts and major changes in technology. Our prosperity and standard of living will depend very much on our vigilance and the speed with which we act. Canada, like other industrial nations, faces a world of increasingly open markets where incredible opportunities are within our grasp. However, the competition for these markets is steadily increasing. We must be prepared for these changes: time is of the essence.
Bill C-21 proposes a comprehensive approach that will help us solve our problems. Bill C-21 updates our
unemployment insurance system while making it possible for more claimants to train for new technologies. Without wishing to be alarmist, we must realize that technological change means our workers must acquire additional skills. We cannot escape this imperative. A day of hesitation is a day lost for the quality of life of our workers.
The message of Bill C-21 and the Labour Force Development Strategy to the people of Canada is this: Be prepared. Prepare for your future. Learn new technologies now.
To young Canadians particularly, we want to say this: Get an education and be prepared to consider training as an on-going process. Madam Speaker, enough time wasted. It is imperative that Bill C-21 be passed and receive Royal Assent. The benefits for Canadians are tremendous. Everywhere I go, I meet people-development officers, workers, unemployed Canadians-who share our views on the Labour Force Development Strategy and Unemployment Insurance reform.
Since 1984, we as a government have started a thorough review of the legislation. Gradually and systematically, we have taken a number of measures whose ultimate goal is to adapt our legislation to the concrete needs of the workers of today and tomorrow. As part of a logical and well-thought out approach, our Labour Force Development Strategy contains four major goals which I may perhaps recall this morning.
First, we want to see a substantial increase in the private sector's role in training these workers and in ensuring that training is more responsive to present labour market needs. We realize it is our role to support the private sector in this very important task: to work with that prime resource, the Canadian labour force.
Second, we have decided to reallocate part of the unemployment insurance budget to increased funding for training and re-employment. Some substantial changes have been made, as we all know, and all these changes will benefit our workers.
Third, we want to improve unemployment insurance benefits, in order to be more responsive to the needs of working parents and workers over 65. The latter are now taking advantage of their right to continue their career, and we must adjust to this new situation.
May 8, 1990

As Minister of State for Seniors, I had an opportunity to talk to this group of workers who want to stay on the job and have a lot of questions about the changes that are urgently needed.
Finally, we want to reduce work disincentives which have tended to make the present system one under which recipients no longer actively seek employment, a situation that has gone on far too long. For each of the goals I just mentioned, we have allocated funding at levels appropriate to new demands and to a modern and pragmatic view of the situation.
Our programs thus include more help for the private sector for human resource planning and training and special assistance for older workers who must relocate. They also provide career training for young people and projects to help revitalize local economies. As a government, we believe in dynamic communities. We are prepared to listen to them and to work in partnership with these communities because they are the only ones who really know their workforce training needs.
As you no doubt know, Madam Speaker, the changes to the old Act reallocate $800 million. These funds will help us launch our labour force development strategy. Once our bill is passed and implemented, there will be more funds for basic training of beginning workers. The funds for the co-operative education program, which is working very well, will be increased fourfold.
Under our proposed changes, $350 million from the UI Fund will be used to increase the aid now given to programs for training, relocation assistance, entrepreneurship and re-employment.
Employers will receive more help for human resource planning. Nearly 41 per cent of full-time workers received no training in the last two years and 53 per cent of unskilled workers receive no training at all. This stagnation worries us because it creates a lack of mobility that harms our economy and runs counter to the present trend of globalization of markets.
In our Bill C-21, we see an opportunity for all Canadians to take a new attitude to their obligation, where they are, to train and retrain throughout their career. As technology changes, Canadians must acquire new skills. Our goal is flexibility.
Government Orders
But we must also note that Bill C-21 is much more than an economic catalyst. This bill faithfully and realistically reflects changes in Canadian society. Finally, the benefits of our new UI plan will comply with our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I am convinced that we have chosen the right path and I am proud to belong to this government that wants to reform this very important social program. We are convinced this is the best way. We chose this approach after repeated consultations with our economic partners. Since 1985, a sound relationship has been established which has helped us acquire specific insights and respond to genuine needs.
Employers, unions, academics and directors of associations convinced us that training was an imperative need. We were mindful of this in developing our reform.
Our bill kills two birds with one stone. First of all, it reinforces the ability of the unemployment insurance system to continue to function as a safety net for people who need it. Second, it provides skills training and offers other specific measures to help claimants adjust to changing labour market conditions.
The new legislation will also change entrance requirements and benefits. These changes reflect wide variations in unemployment across the country. They will mainly benefit claimants living in regions with the highest unemployment rates, where job opportunities are scarce. Where equity had to be restored, we saw to it that it was done.
When the new legislation is passed, claimants will have to accumulate from 10 to 20 weeks of employment to be eligible for benefits, depending on the unemployment rate in the region where they work. This makes for a system that is far more sensitive to unemployment rates and to labour force mobility.
The new legislation will increase penalties for persons who quit without just cause, refuse a suitable job or are fired for misconduct.
The benefit period will be based on the number of weeks of employment and the regional unemployment rate. Flowever, the present three-tier structure will be brought back to a single tier.
We are proposing a complete overhaul of the present system for maternity, sickness and parental benefits. The proposed changes will enhance the flexibility of the benefit system and extend the benefit period, and as I

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
said before, these changes will be in accordance with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Madam Speaker, our new legislation gives workers aged 65 and over the kind of protection they have never had before, because we want to protect the rights of all workers. The people in this age group have no obligation to withdraw from the labour force, and they should be treated fairly. That is what we have done.
Together with our Labour Force Development Strategy, the Canadian Jobs Strategy is a fundamental tool for this government in achieving the main objectives I have mentioned. We have developed six programs, which I will describe briefly.
The Job Development Program was designed to help the long-term unemployed re-enter the job environment with the help of on-the- job training or training in an educational institution.
The Job Entry Program helps people who have trouble entering or re-entering the labour market. It addresses the needs of women, young people and individuals with serious employment problems. Thanks to the UI reform, we have the money to provide additional resources and assistance to reinforce this program for young people, women and the disadvantaged.
We also have the Skill Shortages Program which gives employers the help they need to train employees for jobs where there is a manpower shortage.
The Skill Investment Program is designed for workers who have just been laid off or whose jobs are changing as a result of technological change or developments in the labour market.
The Community Futures Program responds to the needs of small communities experiencing chronic unemployment. We provide training support and assistance for development projects, entrepreneurs and relocation of businesses. The program operates as a partnership with the communities.
Finally, the Innovations Program, as it name indicates, promotes the development and testing of innovative solutions to labour markef pjroblems in specific areas.
The programs I just mentioned are already in effect and will be continued after Bill C-21 is passed. They are
a logical component of our overall approach to unemployment insurance claimants and the various programs we have set up to help them re-enter the labour market as soon as possible and find the jobs they need.
Madam Speaker, adopting Bill C-21 and the Labour Force Development Strategy will make it possible to provide a pragmatic and intelligent solution to many of our labour market problems.
This legislation should be passed without delay. Thousands of unemployed workers and people who are otherwise disadvantaged stand powerless, waiting for the funds the government is prepared to allocate so they can upgrade their training and adjust to the demands of new technologies.
While we hesitate to pass this bill, our competitors continue to step up the training of their workers and to raise their skill levels. Canadian workers deserve better than the present lack of action from Parliament.
Most Canadians, I repeat, approve the direction taken by our government. In a Decima survey, more than 60 per cent of those questioned support updating our unemployment insurance legislation and our options for labour force training. The survey also tells us that more than 90 per cent support what we propose to help claimants find a new job. Eighty-five per cent would support the required changes, as we propose, to give Canada a more qualified labour force.
From having worked with associations of the unemployed before 1984 and from having crossed Canada since 1984,1 personally tell you that the reform before us meets the specific needs of the men and women of Canada.
If we heed the recommendations of experts, the desires expressed by the public, the demands of the global economic reality, we will pass Bill C-21 quickly. Let us do so without delay for the sake of this objective, the quality of life of our Canadian workers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister and her government, in answering the message from the Senate, accepted one important change and the principle of two more, which they will incorporate in the bill.

May 8, 1990

The first amendment adopted, 5(b), deals, as we know, with the unserved period of disqualification imposed on someone who has to, or wishes to, leave a job without valid reason.
The second concerns the training plan to be submitted to the House of Commons for consideration.
The third amendment concerns fishermen's benefits, which, as we know today, are in the regulations and not the legislation. The government agrees to put the regulations on fishermen's benefits into the legislation, which is a step forward.
I must say that we agree with this approach, although these three amendments are very timid, because they are well received by the unemployed and the workers of Canada.
Nevertheless, the government is still hesitating and waffling on the essence of this bill, which is the complete withdrawal of the Canadian government from the financing of unemployment insurance in the years to come.
The burden will thus be borne by the workers and employers, which we do not think is the way to go at all, Madam Speaker, because we believe that the Government of Canada has an important role to play in funding unemployment insurance in the regions with economic difficulties that they cannot face, in some cases, without the help and support of the rest of the country.
I would like to ask the minister a question: The minister knows very well that Bill C-21 is an amendment to the original legislation, the revised 1971 Act. I have already argued in this House, as I am sure the minister knows, that what the Senate wants to do is reduce the present imposition by half. The present legislation provides that the government cover a large part of the cost of unemployment insurance throughout the country.
The Senate proposes that the federal government, instead of eliminating its contribution completely, contribute at least 50 per cent of the cost of benefits.
I ask the minister whether she really has a serious reason to tell Canada's unemployed that the federal government's spending power will no longer benefit them, in order-take note, Madam Speaker-to reduce the deficit. I ask the minister whether this government
Government Orders
wants to wipe out the deficit-and it doubled the debt in the last five years-by saving money on unemployment insurance. How can they justify asking Canadian workers, Madam Speaker, to accept this government's passing the burden of lowering the national debt onto them while withdrawing its spending power for funding unemployment insurance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The answer is very simple, Madam Speaker: It was common sense.
We have known for a number of years that it was imperative to change the unemployment insurance system which, as you said before 1984 and as we have said since then, takes a far too passive approach.
The present government has a number of important objectives to meet, and the Senate's proposal is diametrically opposed to our objectives, which are to reduce the deficit, improve our social programs and reform the unemployment insurance system which we believe is too passive.
What we want to do, in co-operation with employers and workers, is be able to rejuvenate the labour force strategy and prepare that primary resource, our human capital, for the competition we can expect on a global market, and meanwhile achieve part of our initial objective which is to reduce the deficit. Once that has been done, we will be able to improve our social programs.
I know, from having talked to many unemployed workers, that our strategy appeals to Canadian men and women. It appeals to our departmental officers who are ready to work on these training programs.
The strategy appeals to our communities which during the past two years have worked very hard, with the help of volunteers, to define employment and development strategies and make recommendations to the government, recommendations we are now considering and intend to implement.
Bill C-21, while making it possible to reduce the deficit and at the same time maintain a safety net for those who really need it, also provides the resources to reinforce our Jobs Strategy programs, to reinforce this form of partnership with our young workers, and at this point I wish to pay tribute to the energy and enthusiasm of our volunteers, to the people who want to improve

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
conditions in regions beset by unemployment rates that are far too high.
I can say I am proud to belong to a government that has these important objectives and that looks to the future. That is why we are proposing this reform. And if you are so concerned about the well-being of the workers of this country, I suggest you hurry over to the other place and ask your friends to pass Bill C-21 as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister said, but I did not find the comments to be all that convincing.
It is certainly true that the government has run into some trouble with the Senate-let us call it what it is-insofar as the passage of Bill C-21 is concerned. In no way does that excuse the government's lack of action in bringing in the variable entrance requirements, something that has traditionally been done over the last decade, in order to make it possible for people to be able to qualify for unemployment insurance at a lesser period of time than 14 weeks. There is no excuse whatsoever for the government not having done that. It certainly could have brought in other provisions as well, such as parental leave.
I would like to ask the minister specifically: Why was the government so adamant in not bringing in the variable entrance requirements before the end of the year in order that those people who came from regions with high unemployment were not able to access the rates and benefits which in any other year they would have been able to do?

Hon. Monique Ve/.ina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)): For
the simple reason, Madam Speaker, that our bill and our reform contain this sensitivity to unemployment rates that vary from region to region and from sub-region to sub-region. The reform and our bill reflect our concern for peripheral regions with higher unemployment rates.
Madam Speaker, this legislation will help us increase the amount of training we provide, meet specific needs, and be more sensitive to regional unemployment rates.
The variable entrance requirement is included in our unemployment insurance reform because our overall perspective bids us to give special consideration to those regions that are economically sensitive, and we also know that if we are to meet the requirements that will exist in the year 2000, we will have to provide training and do so in co-operation with employers and workers, and that is exactly what we intend to do with our Labour Force Development Strategy and Bill C-21.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Resuming debate with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundurn.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am certainly glad that I did not have to answer the last question which I asked. For the government not to have brought in the variable entrance requirements, which was certainly an option it had, demonstrates the mean and lean and vicious temperament of this government in many different areas of endeavour.
Over a year ago now when Bill C-21 was introduced in this House, the major government propaganda paper that was submitted with it was a piece of garbage called Success in the Workplace. We have had ample opportunity over the last year to see that government members have not been too successful in putting forth the concepts in Bill C-21 and for very good reason. It is not an accident that they find themselves in what may very well turn out to be a constitutional problem with the Senate at this time.
I could not believe it when yesterday, over a year after it had been introduced, the minister said very nearly the same things which had been said a year ago. The vision I had as she was presenting her speech yesterday was that she could hardly contain herself from not hugging herself; she was so pleased with what she was saying and so pleased with what Bill C-21 was supposed to be doing. I cannot believe that after a year she would still feel the same way about such an horrendously bad piece of legislation and something with which the government had so much trouble.
The assurances with which it was introduced have shown to be hollow, and there are a good many reasons why we would conclude that they are so hollow. There
May 8, 1990

were assurances about training and assurances about the training ethic, for heaven's sake, which we may or may not get into later. In case we do not, I will just mention the private sector becoming more involved in the training of Canadian workers. We have not heard too many references to training ethic in relation to Bill C-21 since, with very good reason, because it is something that they are not all that much committed to.
They talk in the most glowing terms of human resource planning. They talk about maternity benefits that are going to accrue under Bill C-21, the benefits to those over 65 years of age and parental benefits, the last two of which except for some change of heart-and I am at a bit of a disadvantage to understand why-were really imposed upon the government as a result of court decisions. As far as the paternal leave was concerned, there was a point up until very shortly before this legislation was introduced where they were going to challenge the decision of the court that parental leave should receive a similar kind of consideration along with adoptive leave. That is just a bit of an indication of how really insincere this government is when it comes to the actions and benefits of Bill C-21.
There are references to the other things to which I have referred such as assistance for social assistance recipients. I would suggest that for the most part every one of those grand and glorious things that they so often fall back on and refer to has very little to do with what Bill C-21 really does. The only way that they can claim any validity as far as Bill C-21 is concerned is that the money they are robbing from those who become unemployed, paid for by those people before they became unemployed, and the money that they are robbing from the UI fund which is now going to go out of the UI fund is totally divorced from Bill C-21. That is why I cannot understand them even referring to these actions within Bill C-21, except that is where they get the money for the training. That is where they are going to get the money for the human resource development. That is where they are going to get the money for Community Futures. That is where they are going to get the money for some of these things that go along with training. That is fine, and we will come to that later.
There are very good reasons those things should occur. However, there are even better reasons those things should not occur in relation to Bill C-21.1 think that the
Government Orders
government is really stretching the credibility of Canadians a long way, particularly those who understand the implications of Bill C-21, to be speaking of them in the same breath at all.
Bill C-21 was introduced with glowing assurances a year ago. It is tremendously fortunate that it has taken Bill C-21 as long as it has to go through this Parliament because it has given us a chance to look at what this government does in relation to other endeavours which it has carried out over the year. We have seen that there is no reason whatsoever to feel any assurance that the benefits the government states will accrue from Bill C-21 will in fact happen.
As with many other things in which the government has involved itself and the Canadian public at the same time, we can only assume that working Canadians and those who become unemployed are in for an extremely rough time. I would suggest that the proof lies in the results of other government actions throughout the year.
When Bill C-21 was first introduced, we had not yet been exposed to the clawbacks. We had not yet realized that this government was so mean spirited that it would be taking back from the children of this country what little accrues to them through the family allowances. We had not realized that our senior citizens, those who had served this country so well and had established many of the principles upon which this country, government and Parliament are based, would have part of their old age pension clawed back.
The government has used closure innumerable times, in relation to Bill C-21 itself and almost every other piece of legislation that has gone through this Parliament. The closure principle within Parliament is one of the meanest, vilest, most desperate measures that governments can use. This government has used closure so often that is becoming almost meaningless to refer to it. In the last year the closure motion was used by this government some 35 times.
The government has introduced clawbacks. What about the sacred trust? There is no reason why the Canadian public should have any faith in this government at all.
The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety was one of the foundations of protection for Canadian workers in this country. It is going to be

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
devastated by cut-backs which this government is going to impose upon the Canadian public.
The reference to the Environics and the Decima poll which claimed that the Canadian public was so much in favour of using UI funds for training is rather amusing. If we are going to talk about polls, let us talk about polls that show how the GST is so unpopular with Canadians and yet the government is certainly not going to back off on that. That is another example of how this government, as it admits, is so entrenched in its philosophical desire to change the social fabric of this country that it will not back off.
There are other examples of why we should not be assured that changes to Bill C-21 are going to be of benefit to Canadians, based on this government's demonstration of animosity toward the Canadian public.
The government that wants to bring in Bill C-21 is so caring and democratic that it arrested two solitary demonstrators outside the entrance to the Elouse of Commons. Would a government that brings in that kind of a regulation and does that to two solitary demonstrators within feet, literally, of this very Chamber, have any particular democratic regard or economic regard for the welfare of Canadian workers and whether or not they are unemployed? I would suggest that the answer is no.
Last December the government brought in back-to-work legislation to force their most disadvantaged employees back to work. These employees were disadvantaged because they were unionized but also because they had been prevented from going on strike ever since the moment they were unionized.
Part of the dispute surrounding that back-to-work legislation was affirmative action. I may be wrong, but it seems to me that yesterday the minister made reference to affirmative action and equal opportunity. I would suggest that any reference to affirmative action and equal opportunity made by the minister yesterday rings particularly hollow and is just that much more of an argument that what the government is proposing to do with Bill C-21 will not meet with success. The government forced workers back to work, mostly women, when tribunal after tribunal had determined that those women had been improperly paid for a long time, and that they
ought to be properly paid. The government forced them back to work without addressing that situation at all.
It is absolutely foolhardy for this government to say that Bill C-21 is going to be beneficial. I would suggest it would be more foolhardy for the Canadian public to ever disabuse themselves of the idea that Bill C-21 is going to be beneficial. I am certain that there is going to be a tremendous amount of hardship wreaked upon the Canadian public when those provisions are brought into force.
The Government implies that once Bill C-21 is passed training will be available to the unemployed, and I would suggest even more particularly to those who have not yet found a job, or to those who will be re-entering the workforce after some time. The implication is that there will be training. They will find that nothing could be farther from the truth.
The very best we can hope for is access to training by a doubling of the number of people who have had access to it in the past. In the past, that number was 3 per cent. At the very maximum, the availability of training for people will be 6 per cent of over a million people who are unemployed, 94 per cent of whom will be thinking they will be able to avail themselves of training only to find out that they will not.
The language with which this bill was introduced and the language with reference to training in this bill is nothing more than trying to get people interested in a lottery.
This government ought to be saying to people that the fact of the matter is that there is a limited amount of money so not everyone will be able to access training. That is the real dishonesty of what this government is doing. Under the present unemployment insurance legislation, if you become unemployed at least you can get unemployment insurance, and to imply that if you become unemployed you will be able to access training is totally dishonest. I would suggest that spending U.I. premiums on training is no way to ensure that people will receive training and it is particularly vicious of this government to make those implications.
The government talks about all this money that is going to be available for training. The question that naturally comes back is, where is the money coming from? The answer is that the money is going to be coming from the victims, those who are going to be unemployed, because they will have to work longer to qualify for less. Employees will have to pay more in
May 8, 1990

premiums and they will receive less, and then the penalties will be increased.
When the bill was first introduced the government said that the abuse of the system was not very high. Whether it was in the committee, whether it has been in this Parliament, as recently as yesterday when the minister made her reintroduction of comments on this bill, the was reference to abuse. I would suggest to this government that if it really believed that doing away with the so-called abuses within the UI system will put people back to work, then the very best thing that could be done would be to do away with UI altogether. If that is the kind of incentive we need to get people back to work, do away with it.
I would suggest that if the government did away with the unemployment insurance scheme, there is not one more person who would find a job. The reason is there are not any jobs out there. It is lack of jobs that is the problem, not that people are abusing the system and not that the fund is necessarily badly abused because people are supposedly drawing more heavily on it than they ought to be.
The incentives which Canadians need to get working are good quality jobs at good quality wages for the single moms, the poorly educated and the illiterate. I know people who are illiterate. I know people who are poorly educated. I know that they are working at jobs that are quality jobs. I know that they are working at jobs at quality wages. There are not a lot of those around any more. Illiterate people are not ignorant people. People who are poorly educated are as able to take their place in Canadian society as anyone else, if the jobs are there for them to do. They are capable of being as gainfully employed as someone who is highly technically trained or professionally trained, and are capable of earning a living if the jobs are there. I am not saying that someone who cannot read should not be given every opportunity to read, but I would suggest that taking funds away from the unemployed is hardly the way to do it.
I suspect that I am running rather short of time. I see that I have one minute. There is so much to be said but I would like to conclude by moving:
Government Orders
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words following the
first word "THAT" and substituting the following therefor:
"The order for the consideration of the amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-21, An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, be discharged and the Bill withdrawn."

speechtext: Questions and comments, the hon. minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to know how the hon.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
member opposite can say, with a straight face, that our proposal is taking funds out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund. He gives the false impression that what we are doing with this legislation is reduce the safety net, which, however, is still in place and will be maintained. He knows perfectly well that the money comes from a transfer of funds within the unemployment insurance system which will help us improve social benefits for workers and provide an incentive for the unemployed to find jobs. My question is this: Since his party is against tax increases and increasing the deficit, how would he consider financing this additional training?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not entirely sure whether I understood the minister's comments. I think I heard the minister say that this was merely a transfer of funds within the unemployment insurance fund. I hope that is not what I heard, because C-21 really does not do that. Bill C-21 removes from the public Treasury any assistance to people who have been working and become unemployed.
Previously, the extended benefits to fishermen came out of general revenue. Previously, other extended benefits as well came from general revenue. If a worker was unemployed and able to access a training program which continued past the expiry date of his or her entitlement to unemployment insurance, the unemployment insurance did not cease. It continued and the continuation of those payments came from general revenue. That will no longer be the case.
In a very real sense, that worker who had been working and contributing to the unemployment insurance fund, at least in some small measure, will be paying a portion of the the cost of his or her own training subsequent to the passage of C-21.
The money the government is always talking about which will be available for training-this $1.3 billion or whatever it is-is money which used to come out of general revenues and went to the direct benefit of the unemployed. That will no longer be there. I have no problem with those on social assistance receiving training. I have no problems with those on social assistance receiving much more social support than they do now.
What I and almost everyone, including employers, who submitted a brief to the parliamentary committee on Bill C-21 objected to was the abuse of funds for those kinds of things, taking it out of the unemployment insurance fund and putting it into there. If the minister meant that it is the juggling of those funds from one side of the Bill C-21 barrier into the public domain, I object to that. If that is what Bill C-21 is doing, then I have been misled and I think the public has as well.
The fact is that the UI fund has now been privatized. The employers and employees who will become the recipients of any benefits from unemployment insurance after Bill C-21 is passed are going to be the ones contributing to it and benefiting from it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What's wrong with that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Well, I may be wrong but-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Of course you are.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I may be wrong in what I am about to say, but I believe that a tremendous amount of public funds goes into the training of lawyers. A tremendous amount of public funds goes into our universities for the training of accountants. A tremendous amount of money even goes to support General Motors and a good many other corporations within our society.
If we can use public funds to train lawyers, we can use public funds to train machinists and mechanics and, yes, labourers, too-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: -because, when one becomes unemployed, one is going to be, quite literally, paying for that trades training out of one's own pocket.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have been treated in the House of Commons to the worst parade of socialist myths that I have heard for some decades. May 8, 1990

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to say just a few words concerning this motion before the House. The Unemployment Insurance Act was changed by the Government of Canada by way of a bill which was rejected in the House of Commons by the opposition parties. That bill went to the Senate which examined it and made amendments.
What does the unemployment insurance bill do? It cuts back on unemployment insurance benefits. It cuts back because the triggering point for receiving unemployment insurance benefits under the new bill is changed so that in most parts of Canada more insurable weeks will be required than are at present. There are no other changes as far as I can see.
We have heard a lot of talk about training and changing the Unemployment Insurance Act so that somebody can be educated or re-educated. I do not see a change in the bill saying that if one wants to attend a vocational school or university one can collect unemployment insurance while going there. The act still states that, if one is attending a full-time course of instruction, one does not qualify under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The Government of Canada turns around and says that it is going to allow certain people to collect unemployment insurance because it is going to buy certain seats in training schools. It does not say that everybody qualifies, as it should say. Therefore, it creates a built-in discrimination against young people and older people. In

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
our vocational and training schools, somebody sitting in one seat is getting unemployment insurance, while the person in the next seat cannot qualify, even though they had worked in the same place.
Anyone who is familiar with the law and jurisprudence surrounding this act, or who has examined the jurisprudence laid down by federal judges-and it amounts to some 12,000 cases in the last 15 years or so-will know that it is veiy confusing. A person entering university will say: "All right, I was working, I am applying for unemployment insurance benefits and I am going to take three courses and maintain my status as a full-time student. I am going to be available for work. I am going to go out and look for employment. I am going to sign a sheet of paper that says that if I can find a job I will leave the school that I am attending."
The law is the law is the law, and the law has not been changed by this government to amend that section of the act that should be amended.
I recall that when the government was campaigning in 1984, it came out with a policy which was right at the top of its policy list to allow people, if they qualified, to collect unemployment insurance benefits while they attended a full-time course of instruction. It was never done, but what a marvellous policy that would be if it was actually implemented.
Every works program of the Government of Canada in Employment and Immigration is under the heading of training. In other words, if you go to work on a works program it is for training for something. If a community wants to receive any type of federal money, it has to be for training somebody to do something.
For example, take a community that is surrounded by forests in which there is a sawmill that has closed. The community applies for a works program for a year to thin the forests. Under this government, the only people who qualify to go to work in the woods are people who have never been in the woods before.
The whole structure of job creation has changed under this government so that the only work available through the Government of Canada in a logging community is for non-loggers who are going {p be trained to become loggers when all the other loggers are out of work. Or you might find 10 or 12 out-of-work carpenters in a small community where a job comes up to build a public
building, but they are not allowed to work on that project because they are already carpenters.
Because all of the money for works programs is zeroed in on high unemployment areas, you find that the very people who are out of work and who need work cannot go to work. You put more people into that vocation to put them out of work because once they have worked at it for one year they are not allowed to work at it for the next year.
This business of training really has no justification at all as a positive measure under this particular bill. The average unemployment insurance cheque in Canada today is about $204.50. Imagine, Madam Speaker, all the people abusing that system. Imagine abusing the system to collect $204 when, depending upon your circumstances, you would qualify for almost that amount of social security, depending upon which province you live in.
The list of cases of abuse that were just referred to are commonly identified as overpayments by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Auditor General. The principal cause of overpayments in Canada is a mistake by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act, if the commission makes a mistake, or if the employer makes a mistake on his books, it is registered as an overpayment and the amount of the overpayment is to be paid back by the recipient.
Most of the overpayments were caused by mistakes by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, or by the employer. What is this poor person supposed to do who is getting $204 a week, the average unemployment insurance cheque?
By the way, the total number of people receiving unemployment insurance in Newfoundland today is about 120,000. There are only 240,000 in the workforce, yet this government claims that the unemployment rate is somewhere around 12 per cent. The hon. gentleman is finding that difficult to understand. In some provinces when the unemployment rate goes down, the total number of unemployment insurance recipients goes up. It is interesting, if you are doing a budgetary analysis, to be asking for more unemployment insurance money
May 8, 1990

because your unemployment rate had actually gone down. The reason for that, of course, is that it is short-term employment. When you have an increase in short-term employment you also have a subsequent increase in the number of people collecting unemployment insurance benefits.
Just imagine saying that there is a lot of cheating going on, that people are using the system. What are they using the system for, to get 60 per cent of their wages to a maximum of less than $400 a week? That is quite a using of the system. A straight investigation would find that the cause for these overpayments is not the people themselves, but some mistake by the commission or the employer.
I noticed another misconception. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans went down to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia the other day and said on national television that people enter the fishery and work for 10 weeks and then they go home and sit down for 42 weeks. And he said: "Is that the kind of example that we want our young people in Canada to follow?"
For the information of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, nobody, not one fisherman in Canada, ever worked for 10 weeks and sat home for 42 weeks. Never has one and never will one. Of course, the reason for that is quite simple. You see, when you are a fisherman you can only collect unemployment insurance benefits from the middle of November to the middle of May.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans had a press conference on national television and said that fishermen work for 10 weeks and sit home for 42 weeks. Every fisherman scratched his head and said: "How can I do that when I can only collect for six months under the law of the land?"
