speechtext: Be a fish plant worker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is not a fisherman, it is a fish plant worker. There is quite a distinction.
As far as changes are concerned, hon. members on the government side said, "We want to change the Unemployment Insurance Act". How about changing it to make it fairer, to end the discrimination that is built into the act that has arisen from recent changes made by the
Government Orders
Government of Canada? As I suggested before, why not make everybody eligible for unemployment insurance benefits if they are attending a full-time course of instruction to educate themselves? Why not change the fisheries regulations to make them exactly the same as labour legislation and allow fishermen to draw unemployment insurance as any labourer or fish plant worker does? Why discriminate against a fisherman and not only limit him to November to May but also take 25 per cent off the top if he is a boat owner? There is built-in discrimination in the act.
There are some things that it is not necessary to change. The section of the act relating to someone who quits is being amended. The government is saying that instead of a six-week penalty there is going to be an eight-week penalty. That really does not mean anything under the law because it is the Unemployment Insurance Commission that determines the period of time, from one week to six weeks under present legislation, that a person is going to lose if they quit their employment without just cause.
The definition of "just cause" under the act is very explicit. The commission may say that person had good cause but did not have just cause and so is going to be penalized for two, three or four weeks. Sometimes you see a six-week disqualification, although not very often because you would have to be kind of stupid to quit your work to collect unemployment insurance at 60 per cent of what you were making, a cheque of, on average, $200 a week. So there usually is some cause involved.
There are sections of the act that should be changed, that it would be very simple to change. I have always suggested over the years that we ask the ultimate experts on the Unemployment Insurance Act what changes to make. There is one group of people who are experts on the Unemployment Insurance Act. They are justices of our courts.
Justice Dubinsky from Nova Scotia recently passed away. He was a learned gentleman who knew the Unemployment Insurance Act perhaps better than anybody in Canada knows the act. There are many other justices who know the act inside out. There is Justice Martin and other justices who could be consulted and asked what changes should be made.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
Why is it that members of Parliament sit in their offices and do nothing about it? It is because they do not know what to do about it. Thke, for example, the case of a man who was working, took sick, and had to go on disability. His place of employment had what is commonly referred to as wage loss insurance or short-term disability through an insurance company, or workman's compensation. There are thousands of cases that are referred to MPs every year.
The gentleman has a short-term disability of 15 weeks. Then he applies for unemployment insurance benefits, but these benefits are based on the top-up in sick pay given by his employer. In other words, after working all his life and then becoming disabled, he ends up with anywhere from $50 to $150 a week unemployment insurance until he can get his long-term disability resolved.
Under the Unemployment Insurance Act, it would be quite simple to introduce an amendment that would say: "Your unemployment insurance benefits would be based on your previous 20 weeks of employment with the company with which you were actually working", as it presently states in the act. There are numerous changes that can be made by the Government of Canada in the abduction sections of the act, but the only changes it made were to save money, to cut back on the benefits and to say: "You are going to qualify for unemployment insurance now, depending on which side of the line you live." This sets communities against communities.
Provinces have never before seen such division with people who are applying for unemployment insurance benefits.
This is an absolutely terrible bill. We commend the people who object to this legislation, and we ask the Government of Canada to accept the repeater provision immediately so that the people in high unemployment areas can collect unemployment insurance benefits with the bare minimum waiting period of 10 weeks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
As I join in this debate. Madam Speaker, I should like to thank the Government House Leader for giving us a copy of the government response to the last Senate message this past Friday after my request in the House. 1 am grateful
to him because at least we had a chance to consider the government reaction and to familiarize ourselves with the rather complicated provisions contained in this document.
Now then, the speech delivered yesterday by the Minister of Employment and Immigration leads me to the conclusion that the government has paid precious little attention to the debates that have taken place in both the House and the Senate. Its very timid response tells us once again that the government has a one-track mind when it comes to accepting or amending the amendments duly advocated in the Senate message. The unemployment insurance legislation would definitely be improved if these amendments were accepted.
One significant fact is that this is a first for the House of Commons, a historic first in parliamentary life: a response to a message from the Senate has been sent back to us for the second time with what are basically the same amendments, if we exclude those that have been adopted in a previous debate.

When the story on Bill C-21 is reviewed in years to come, it will be seen as one of the most bizarre episodes in the history of this House. Parliamentarians will treat it as a case study on how not to proceed with important pieces of legislation.
Briefly, I want to recall the events starting with March 20, 1990 when we received a message from the Senate telling us that it was insisting on the passage of its amendments to Bill C-21, the unemployment insurance legislation. These amendments were the same ones that were either amended or rejected by the Conservative majority in this House on March 13, 1990.
Instead of dealing with the latest message from the Senate in a substantive way, the government House leader attempted to resolve his political problem by appealing to the Speaker on what cannot be assessed as anything else but spurious procedural grounds. There was nothing before the House, yet he rose on a point of order.
He was allowed to put a long diatribe on the record, contesting the validity of the acceptability of the amendments, and wanted the Speaker to rule them out of order, but the Speaker refused to bail him out. We are now back in the same position that we were in more than
May 8, 1990

a month ago, that is debating the message with amendments that are in order.
The government now proposes to send another message to the Senate, a copy of which will be appended to today's minutes for those who have time and want to read them. They will find that the government is telling senators that it agrees with a few of the amendments but disagrees with most of them.
I could not find any precedent over the weekend of how the House of Commons responds to messages from the Senate. There is no precedent for the procedure now being proposed by the government House leader. I looked in Beauchesne and found that citation 814 describes the procedure for dealing with Senate amendments. It reads as follows:
814. When the House of Commons does not agree to the Senate amendments, it adopts a motion which states reasons for its disagreement. This is communicated to the Senate.
We did this on March 13. Beauchesne goes on:
If the Senators persist in their amendments, they send a message
informing the House of this fact.
We received that message, as I said, on March 20. Beauchesne continues:
Upon this, -
That is, receipt of the message from the Senate:
- the House either accepts the amendments or adopts a motion requesting a conference to which each House appoints Members; and a date is fixed for their meeting.
That is part of citation 814. The options provided by Beauchesne when the Senate insists are to either accept the amendments or request a conference.
We cannot go on with this kind of ping-pong game, messages flying from the Senate to the House of Commons, and back and forth. Maybe badminton is a better example than ping-pong; nevertheless, it sounds to me as if we are into a process of tit for tat. That has to come to an end some time.
I would like to continue with the citation from Beauchesne to describe what happens if no agreement is reached at the conference which, in our view, should be called and asked for by the House. I read from Beau-chesne's fifth edition, at page 241:
Should they again disagree, the House may accept the amendments
or the Senate may withdraw them, but when neither of these courses is
followed, no further action is taken on the bill.
Government Orders
That is the process that has been with us for more than 100 years, and that is the way things usually work out.
It is well described in, I think, Standing Order 57 and in Beauchesne's fifth edition under the heading "Appendix 1, Forms and Formulae", page 283, where the forms which would be used in this event can be found.
This procedure of holding a conference is one that the government House leader is desperately trying to avoid. Although it is provided for in our Standing Orders and is found in all the authorities, the government wants nothing to do with it. It even suggests that this is antiquated procedure not in keeping with modern parliamentary practice. I would say bunk to that. The truth is that though conferences have been available since Confederation, they were first used only at the turn of the century and have been used sometimes since then. Those who are not familiar with the process could look it up. I could give them a long speech as I have all kinds of notes on the conference and how it should be held and how it is to be proposed. But I will not dwell on that today because this may get the government all excited and disturbed.
I want to get back to the message. The government House leader has argued in the House against amendments 5(a), 5(b), 7 and 9 on various grounds. I submit humbly that all his arguments are invalid.
The minister asserts that the amendments are contrary to the principle of the bill. A bill may have only one principle. Otherwise amendments to the clauses would be in order at second reading if it had several principles.
As stated in Beauchesne's, citation 764, subparagraph 3: "The principle of a bill is stated in its long title". The government House leader seemed to think that a bill can have several principles. For example, at page 10140 of Hansard, he speaks of a "major principle of Bill C-21" and alluded there were others. He stated that amendments 7 and 9 "are clearly contrary to that principle of the bill". However, he then says, and I quote: "For the Senate to insist upon amendments that essentially undo or negate the principles of Bill C-21-" and he goes on. There cannot be any more than one principle.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
I ask the minister, since he used the plural, how many principles does this bill have? If a bill can have more than one principle it follows that it should be possible to vote, "no" to one principle on second reading, and "yes" to another, if he could only find them. There is only one principle.
The Speaker himself in his decision stated that the principle of Bill C-21 is to discontinue government support of the unemployment insurance account. That is one principle that is within the bill.
If you read Bill C-21, there is more to it than that. Many clauses of the bill, if we had to deal with only the principle enunciated the other day, would have to be removed from Bill C-21. For example, those dealing with training and development, retraining programs, and all kinds of other things which do not have anything to do with discontinuing government support of the unemployment insurance account.
Unless we return to the time tested proposition that a bill has only one principle, that the Flouse votes on only one principle at second reading, the whole legislative process would be chaotic and meaningless.
As Beauchesne's states, the principle is stated in the long title of the bill. The long title of Bill C-21 reads:
An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the
Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.
That is what this House undertook to consider when it gave Bill C-21 second reading.

According to the Government House Leader, Madam Speaker, the Senate amendments fly in the face of the government's budget policies. He argues that the bill is based on government budget policies approved by the House, and he maintains that the Senate does not have the constitutional authority to amend it. What a strange argument, Madam Speaker. The minister claims that the budget vote carries a number of consequences. In his remarks he stated that the vote on the budget was tantamount to automatic clearance to collect taxes. Not true. Taxes are levied against the population, not by a budget resolution but through the legislative process by acts of Parliament. We have no statute like Britain's Provisional Collection of Taxes Act 1913. The minister may have drawn inspiration from that legislation, but we do not have anything like it in Canada, it is a British statute.
Never has anyone dared to suggest that it applies to Canada.
Then, the Minister claimed that in the case of a budget motion, it is unconstitutional for the Senate to amend Bill C-21 through amendments 5(a), 5(b), 7 and 9.
Madam Speaker, based on that reasonning, had the Senate simply rejected Bill C-21, those amendments would still have been unconstitutional. Even the Minister did not venture to state that openly. However, it is perfectly obvious that those amendments run contrary to the approved budgetary policies of the government. The same holds true for amendments made by the House, Madam Speaker.
Of course, the government House leader is of the opinion that the simplest budget motion referred to in the Standing Orders has an enormous constitutional impact. According to him, that allows the government to levy taxes. That changes the Constitutional Act of 1867, making it possible to force the Senate to adopt all bills relating to budgetary policies as they are approved by the House of Commons.
Madam Speaker, that confines that House to amending money bills. Is there the slightest hint of truth in what the government is saying?

I want to allude to the procedure that was followed prior to December 1968 because it is important. At that time the Minister of Finance presented his budget statement on the motion that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into a committee of Ways and Means. If after the budget debate that motion carried, the House went into the committee of Ways and Means to consider the several Ways and Means motions tabled by the Minister of Finance at the end of his statement. When a Ways and Means motion had been carried in committee, a bill to give legal effect to the motion was formulated by the minister. Thus, every tax bill originated in the House of Commons as required by Section 53 of the Constitutional Act, 1867.
The constant complaint against that procedure was that tax measures were being debated at least three times. They were debated during the budget debate, in the committee of Ways and Means, and at the several stages of the bills. In the 1960s the House decided to eliminate the Ways and Means stage. This meant that the House would not go into a committee of Ways and Means. This meant that the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair was pointless. The House provided a new form. It replaced that the Speaker do now leave the chair
May 8, 1990

with, and I read: "That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government".
This new motion has no more legislative or constitutional significance than the old one. If carried, it means that the House has not withdrawn its confidence from the government, but it does not modify the constitutional powers of either the House of Commons or the Senate when tax bills originated by Ways and Means motions are before Parliament.

In any case, Bill C-21 is not a money bill. Such bills must originate in the House of Commons, following a vote on a Ways and Means motion which is non debatable, as we know, since 1968.
As far as I know, Madam Speaker, no Ways and Means motion relating to Bill C-21 was tabled. The minister knows all that. He knows that Bill C-21 is not a money bill. He knows that, even if it were, a vote does note affect the powers of the House or that of the Senate.

What is he trying to prove? I asked the minister to show me where the Ways and Means motion was put to the House dealing with Bill C-21. There just isn't any, Madam Speaker. It was a statutory bill voted in 1971 which established a reformed system of unemployment insurance that we modified by having before the House Bill C-21. It was an amendment to the bill of 1971; not a Ways and Means motion but a statutory amendment. It is not renewed in Ways and Means motions by Estimates every year.
We will never find that in the Estimates, anymore than we will find the moneys required for paying family allowances or old age security pensions. These are statutory programs which the government has to follow every year. They do not come to us with Ways and Means or Estimates every year saying that we would like to have the House of Commons do this. That is an engagement. It is something we do every year and that the government knows very well is the way we operate.
Government Orders
I turn now to the matter of the Royal recommendation and the financial initiative of the Crown. What Bill C-21 does in the clauses amended by 5(a), 5(b), 7, and 9 is reduce the statutory charges made by the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-72. The Speaker, at the time he made his ruling, stated on April 26, 1990 that it would be in order for this House to restore the charges on the Consolidated Revenue Fund that are being reduced or cancelled by Bill C-21. I want to quote the Speaker:
It could certainly be permissible in this House to restore in an amending bill charges already provided for in existing legislation. For guidance on that point, I refer hon. members to Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, 21st edition, page 716 -
It is under the heading of matters involving money which do not require the Queen's recommendation and in a sense answers the question as to the constitutionality of the process.
It would have been in order for a member of this House to have moved amendment 7 at the report stage, for example. It could have been done in this House at report stage, not before. The charges that Bill C-21 would reduce or cancel exist today. They are authorized by law. Nobody is trying to reduce the financial initiative of the Crown. The Crown has an unquestioned right to initiate tax and appropriation bills, but the fact that the Crown has the sole right to initiate does not restrict the power of this House, or the Senate for that matter, to amend or refuse to pass those bills. The power to initiate is not the power to legislate.

Madam Speaker, the Government House Leader is complaining that the Senate's amendments would reduce the financial initiatives of the Crown. Nothing could be farther from the truth, which is that the Government originally mismanaged the changes it wanted to make to the unemployment insurance scheme. It should have introduced a bill to repeal the previous legislation from a date to be determined by proclamation. In this "way, it could have proposed immediately the kind of unemployment insurance scheme it wanted, and the royal recommendation would have accompanied a new bill which would have been binding on both of the House of Commons and the Senate. But the Govern-

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
ment botched up the whole thing. It has been stuck ever since in a procedural mess and has made fruitless efforts to regain some credibility and remedy the situation.
Madam Speaker, you will remember that the Speaker of the House himself had referred in a moving fashion to the Act of Parliament of 1911. Since this British statute was deemed relevant, allow me to make a few short comments on this legislation.

Let us suppose, Madam Speaker, that we have in Canada a comparable law. Would its provisions concerning money bills have helped the government get Bill C-21 enacted? They would not. The Parliament Act, 1911, defines money bills very precisely.
Money bills are those that tax, appropriate money, authorize borrowing. Nothing other than those specified matters may be included. Bill C-21 is not a money bill. Erskine May's twenty-first edition, page 751, defines a money bill and I refer members to that quotation.
Madam Speaker, I see you are going to rise and tell me that my time is up. I tell you, Madam Speaker, the government is on the wrong line of this one. I think it should accept the message from the Senate, go with it and have a better bill. I only wish that it would come to its senses.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to put a few comments on the record and a question. The previous speaker to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier who has just completed his remarks made an incredible statement that I think cannot go unchallenged. He said that Bill C-21 was invented in an ivory tower without consultation. That is an incredible statement.
There was a task force on unemployment insurance that was produced in 1981-82 on unemployment insurance. There was the Macdonald Commission report in 1985. The Forget Commission tabled its report in 1987, and the legislative committee on Bill C-21 consulted all over the country with more than 200 groups and individuals.
Certainly it is not a bill that was produced in an ivory tower. Years of study preceded this bill, and the government has proposed a plan that does what is possible today and not tomorrow. Workers want help now, not in some theoretical future. So much for what he had to say.
I would like to comment on what the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier said. I am amazed because he portrays himself as a House of Commons man. He regularly quotes Beauchesne's and Erskine May and balances the Standing Orders on his head. He made not one comment on the Speaker's ruling. It really surprised me that he would not comment on that.
I thought he would have at least commented on the method the Senate is trying to use to bootleg in amendments to a bill which we would not accept in committee under the rules of the House or we would not accept in the House of Commons under the rules of the House. He seems to think that they are quite appropriate if they are bootlegged by the Senate. I thought he would have commented on that.
He said: "The power to initiate is not the power to legislate". That is an incredible statement. Why would you initiate anything? Would it be just for the exercise of running around in circles? You cannot legislate unless you do initiate, so we initiated the bill and want to see it put into place.
I might refer briefly to the Speaker's ruling on April 26 on page 10726 of Hansard:
I also draw to the attention of my colleagues-and I know they will be very interested -on both sides of the House to hear the comments by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on September 7, 1917. As I say, this is not put in as the substance of the ruling. It is just brought to members' attention, and I hope the attention of every Canadian who has a chance to listen or read this judgment. This is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said on September 7, 1917.
This was his view. He was a great House of Commons man: "Under Rule 78, the Senate has no right to amend or alter in any way a money bill sent to them from this House". Rule 78 is the same as our Rule 80 paragraph 1.
He said: "This House alone has the privilege of dealing with money bills. The only right the Senate has is that of rejecting or assenting to such money bills. That rule has been confirmed over and over again in England".
I am rather surprised. My hon. colleague, for whom I have a great deal of affection, has promoted the independence of the House of Commons and has spoken in complimentary terms many times about this place. He speaks about how we should protect our rights and privileges, but he seems to have brushed that all aside in his speed to approve what the Senate is trying to bootleg
May 8, 1990

through this House. I just wish he would perhaps comment on that.
He seems to make light of the fact that we have accepted some amendments put forth by the Senate. He knows very well that this is the normal ebb and flow of views. He knows as well that there was a time when the Senate would get a bill at eleven o'clock in the morning and pass it by twelve o'clock; that is when the Liberals were in power as as government.
In fact, if we look at the last bill that went through the House under the Liberals on unemployment insurance, I think it took a total of two and one-quarter hours to run it through the Senate in all readings and bring it back to the House. It was a same day ruling. Suddenly all these things are swept aside and the member seems to feel that we should not accept any of the rulings that the Senate has put forward. In fact he has commented that to accept any of them means that we should accept all of them. I wonder if the member could comment on that. I have given him enough avenues to run down that he probably will go on for another hour.

Madam Speaker, I would be more than pleased to do that. I see the member has done his research and I commend him for it. I have the same documents from which he was reading. I just want to remind him that in reading the documents he must at least-and I know him to be an honest person-give exactly the context in which it was put.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was talking at that time about aids and supplies. Aids and supplies is not before the House with Bill C-21. He knows that and I know that. This has nothing to do with Estimates. I addressed that in my comments. This has to do with statutory obligations of the government, bills that encompass expenditures from funds of the government of Canada, and has nothing to do with aids and supplies. I addressed that in my first comments and I address it again.
Since he did bring up the issue, and to any member interested in reading the debate that day, the Speaker of the House was a former member for the Gaspe riding, with which my grandfather had something to do, and his name was Rodolphe Lemieux. There would be some
Government Orders
historical events here which I could relate to my friend some time when he is interested in hearing about it. I know Madam Speaker knows all about Rodolphe Lemieux and how close he was to the Gauthier family. I will not say any more than that.
Having dealt with the issue of what was not dealt with in the debate, I would like to throw back to the member the comment made by his own minister responsible for government House business, on the Question Period program of Sunday last, May 6, 1990, at 6 p.m. I just want to quote one phrase from that because it deals somewhat with what the member was talking about, the Senate's authority.
I want to quote the House Leader on the government side, who said: "You see, the Senate's authority comes from a clause in the Canadian Constitution that says there will be a Parliament consisting of the Queen, the Senate, and the House of Commons.
Now, the Governor General has the same powers the Senate is claiming but everybody would be quite surprised, to say the least, if the Governor General said: 'Well, I am going to amend this legislation before passing it'."
Madam Speaker, we know that is nonsense. The Governor General does not have the same powers that the Senate has. The Senate is a legislative body; the Governor General is not a legislative body. If the government thinks that the Governor General has the same power as the Senate, I would put the following scenario: if the government went to the Governor General and asked the Governor General to give Royal Assent to Bill C-21, and the Governor General said: "I don't like the bill, Mr. Prime Minister". Well, that would have the effect of telling the Prime Minister, "Find yourself another job. I just fired you".
He would have lost the confidence of the Governor General. Mind you, there is the other side of the story. The Prime Minister could call the Queen and say: "Your Royal Highness, fire that Governor General". We could have that kind of fight, but that is not the way things run around here. The Governor General has a role to play, within the triumvirate, if you like, of parliament's constitutional obligations.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
It is there as part of our system, but he does not have the same powers as the Senate. The difference is that the Senate has the power to amend legislation and that is what it has done here; it has proposed good amendments, we think, to Bill C-21. For reasons I do not understand, the government fails to recognize that the arguments we are making are good, sound, and acceptable, and in order.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to rise and speak in this debate, in support of those amendments sent to us from the other place. I wish to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, for his cogent arguments on behalf of the acceptance of those amendments.
I wish to speak a bit, today, about the region from which I come, the Atlantic region, and what it is to be an Atlantic Canadian. I wish to speak about what the policies of this government, including the policies that have resulted in the government's version of Bill C-21, are doing to Atlantic Canadians.
I sat here yesterday in this Elouse and listened to various hon. members, including the hon. parliamentary secretary, and I think that in spite of the number of Atlantic Canadians, which number 32 in this House, sometimes members from other parts of the country are not quite so aware of what it is and what it means to come from that small region of this country.
In our history in the Atlantic region we have been coal miners, in the fishery, farmers, small business operators and loggers. There has been a very diversified but small-based economy in the Atlantic region. A great deal of the work done in Atlantic Canada in those four provinces depends upon the season of the year.
Without going into all the trials and tribulations of the fishing industry, we have seen that in various parts of the Atlantic region, fishing is a seasonal occupation. Clearly because of our climate, farming is a seasonal occupation. Unfortunately, the coal mines are dead and have long been dead. This is the product of policies of yet another Conservative government and I cannot get into the problems inherent in that industry. We have a problem in Cape Breton Island with the steel plant. We have problems throughout Atlantic Canada and Atlantic Canadians rightly, are feeling hard done by. Rightly, Mr. Speaker, Atlantic Canadians sit back and wonder about this government and how it feels about them.
My hon. friend across the way yesterday talked about the fact that Lockeport, Nova Scotia could get in line along with a number of other communities for programs under this bill. I ask the hon. member, as I am reasonably certain if I leave him enough time he will probably make some comment, what he sees as the alternative for the town of Lockeport. It is a one-industry town, I think he would agree with me on that, and that industry is based in the fishery. It is based on the fishery whether you are talking about those who go out to fish, who can no longer do so, or those who process the fish in the plant that is now closed.
I heard yesterday from various members of this House on the government side and I read last night about some journalists who adhere to the government's position. They were talking about the fact that the theory that we have called, on this side of the House, the move or starve theory, but they will not use words quite as blunt as that. They were saying that the move or starve theory is one that Canadians just have to adjust to. This is why I say there is some lack of understanding about Atlantic Canadians by some of the other members of this House.
We have been moving out of Atlantic Canada practically since the first Europeans landed there in 1604. Atlantic Canadians are very attached to the place where they were born and to the place where their roots are. I am not suggesting that Ontarians, Quebecois, westerners and northerners are not just as attached but let them make their arguments when they stand in this House. I am speaking now for the people I represent and for the people from the whole region from which I am fortunate enough to come. But to say that we have no comprehension of the economic realities of life and to say that it is enough to walk into Lockeport, Canso, Sydney Mines or Halifax and say, "Well, if you can't get a job, move out", is to show a total lack of sensitivity and a total lack of awareness about what this country stands for.
While growing up in this country, I saw lots of my friends and classmates move. I saw them go to Calgary and Edmonton and other places in western Canada during the oil boom. I saw them move to Windsor, Ontario to help build cars. I saw them move to the mines in Ontario when the coal mines in Cape Breton closed. There is nothing you can tell someone from Atlantic
May 8, 1990

Canada about moving out because there are no jobs. We have been doing that over and over again.
This government promised something better to Atlantic Canadians in 1984. It tried to promise the same thing in 1988 with, I am happy to say, a little less success.
This is not something on which we base partisan politics. This is the root of Canadianism and the root of what makes our country strong, the fact that every young Canadian should be able to choose to stay reasonably close to the place where he or she was born and grew up. You should not have to move to Toronto to have a better life. You should not have to move to Calgary, or Vancouver, or Montreal. You should be able to do it in small town Canada, in rural Canada, whether it be Saskatchewan or New Brunswick, Newfoundland or the Northwest Territories.
That is not what we are seeing today. We are seeing a systematic breakdown of this country. We are seeing this country turned into huge urban centres and small town Canada and rural Canada going by the boards. One of the ways in which this is being done is through the attempted passage of this bill in the form in which the government brought it.
Mr. Speaker, I ask you to look at the statistics, the unemployment rates and the entrance requirements under the old unemployment insurance scheme and under the new. I ask you to look at my own riding of Halifax. The unemployment rate in Halifax is approximately 7.8 per cent.
I might add that my learned colleague from Dartmouth is not with us at the moment. He and I frequently have the discussion that because of the small areas in Atlantic Canada different places get lumped in together, and that is exactly what happens in the unemployment statistics. The city of Halifax actually has a higher unemployment rate but because the slightly more prosperous city of Dartmouth is lumped in, along with the suburban areas, the Halifax figures look a little bit better. In actual fact, unemployment in the urban area and in my riding of Halifax is not as low as 7.8 per cent. I merely bring that up for information.
Government Orders
The entrance requirements under the old scheme call for 12 weeks. The entrance requirements under the new scheme call for 18 weeks. The number of weeks for which you can collect benefits under the old scheme was 28 weeks and under the new scheme is 21 weeks.
An unemployed human being is an unemployed human being. Just because there is a need to make the books look better from the government point of view, why should the requirements become so much stiffer in an area that is generally economically slower than anywhere else in the country? Six more weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance is going to prevent people from ever being able to collect benefits. A twenty-eight week benefit as opposed to a 21-week benefit means that many people who do manage to qualify will hardly be able to get themselves through the difficult winter periods. In Atlantic Canada, because so much work is seasonal, a great deal of the insurable weeks is maintained through the summer months. It is maintained because of the additional work in the tourism industry, in the entertainment industry, and so on.
It is a question of fairness and understanding of what people want to do. I attended a meeting where people talked about stereotypes. They said that Canadians did not want to be stereotyped according to cultural background or according to various and sundry other criteria. I said at the time that we in Atlantic Canada were used to being stereotyped. We were used to the stereotype of Atlantic Canadians sitting on a wharf in the fog, spitting into the water, and waiting for the unemployment insurance cheques to roll in. That stereotype is as pernicious as any other stereotype.
Atlantic Canadians are hard workers. That is one of the reasons they have moved so frequently to other parts of the country. They come from backgrounds of coalminers, fishermen, farmers, steel plant workers, dock workers in Halifax-backgrounds of hard work and physical labour.
I might also add that something that has long been established in the country is the brain-drain from Atlantic Canada. Our wonderful universities in those four provinces have sent people to other universities, to this House, and to the courts right across Canada. They have led the way academically and professionally for many other Canadians. However, we do not dwell on that

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
because we are modest people and do not blow our own horns too much of the time.
This stereotype of Atlantic Canadians just trying to get 10 weeks of insurable earnings so they can sit around, allegedly, and collect unemployment insurance for the rest of the time is unacceptable. In my belief and in the belief of many of my colleagues on this side of the House, it is this kind of attitude that created this legislation.
I recall a man I dealt with back in Nova Scotia. He did not come from my riding but was from rural Nova Scotia. He was one of the hardest workers I have seen. During the spring and fall, he worked in the woods doing as much logging as he could, given the limited resources of that industry in Nova Scotia. In the late fall he worked cutting Christmas trees for export. In the summer he did some commercial fishing when it was available. And in the winter when he could not go into the woods and he could not fish, he would hitch-hike 20 miles into the town nearest his home in the country to shovel snow for people who lived there. He hired himself out as a handyman and generally did any job that came along. If there was any work available, this man would take it. And he was not unusual. I know thousands of Nova Scotians who are like that. They try as best they can to survive in a mixed economy.
But with the mixed economies of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland, from mid-December pretty well until mid-April, there just are no jobs in many parts of our provinces.
These people work from mid-April to mid-December at a variety of other jobs. They pay into unemployment insurance. Of course, they would rather be working. Any human being who has a modicum of self-respect wants to be able to support himself or herself and to provide for his or her family. That is absolutely endemic to the human condition.
But again, in looking at this bill, it is as if the government is saying: "We do not trust you out there. We know that you do not really adhere to the work ethic that we do, and we are going to get you. We are going to show you that you cannot possibly get away with all the things you have been getting away with for so long."
It says to us on this side of the House that we have a government that does not think very highly of its own citizens, and thinks even less highly if those citizens
happen to come from the four small provinces clinging to the Atlantic sea coast.
When the other place made these amendments and sent them back to us, as was its right to do, I think that there was perhaps a glimmer of hope, certainly among the people whom I represent. The response to this bill in the Atlantic has not been favourable, not at all.
I participated in some of the committee hearings in Halifax last summer and while we were sitting, another committee was set up by a group of concerned citizens to hear all the people who could not come before the legislative committee. My colleagues and I from the opposition side went to that committee as well to hear what these people had to say. They had not had the opportunity to speak to the members of parliament because time was so limited.
The stories from these people about the lives that they live and the impact the changes in this bill will have on their lives were incredibly moving and frightening. It is because of this, and because of the amendments sent to us from the other place, that I think there is some hope. The other place is supposed to be the chamber of sober second thought.
For those opposite who have been bemoaning the fact that the other place does its job, I might add that the other place is a duly constituted, constitutional body. It has a job to do and it is doing it. I say to my colleagues on the government side: "You are the ones with the majority. If you do not like it, change it. You have the power to do so." But they are not doing so. Instead, they are taking things one step too far and taking it out on the citizens of Canada, particularly on the citizens of Atlantic Canada.
When Bill C-21 was first debated in the Chamber, it was not debated long enough. Every member of Parliament did not have the time they should have had in order to make his or her views known and to represent the people of the country.
There has been a great deal of talk, as well, about the Senate's delays. Again, I think that this is unfair. What the other place has done, has been done in its usual manner. The hon. parliamentary secretary talked about the fact that, under a previous government, the other place would pass bills as quickly as an hour and a half or two and a half hours. I merely state, for his own
May 8, 1990

edification, that I guess they know good legislation when they see it.
We know the bill was not sufficiently debated in the House of Commons and we know, as I said before, that many groups did not have the opportunity to be heard. Provincial governments were not heard by the House committee. Claude Forget, the former chairman of the royal commission on unemployment insurance was not heard. The Economic Council was not heard, and so on. It was insufficient. Is it any wonder that the other place, knowing its duty as the Chamber of sober second thought, was not prepared to ram this through in the manner prescribed by the government?
The hearings on Bill C-21 were organized hurriedly during the summer. Again, numerous groups which applied to be heard were not permitted to be heard, giving rise to the kind of "anti-hearings" that were held in Halifax. This bill had to be reported back to the House by October 6. Everybody knows that if you want to get something through without Canadians noticing, do it in the summer time. That is what happened and, with that sort of timetable, the committee spent only one day in every province other than Ontario and Quebec, where two days were spent. That is not very much time to hear the views of those who represent over 25 million Canadians.
The other thing is that this legislation is complex. It is difficult enough for members of Parliament-some of them at any rate-to grasp what this bill is all about, let alone members of the general public, who do not have the resources or the assistance that we have, to grasp what it is we are dealing with.
The major thing is that Bill C-21 cuts $1.5 billion from regular benefits and ends the government's contribution to unemployment insurance which, last year, was $2.8 billion. These changes are radical and they should be given very close examination. In light of the radical nature of these changes, the groups that are affected by these changes should have had every opportunity to express their views.
One thing I found particularly upsetting was with regard to the variable entrance requirements and what took place in the House last December. My riding of Halifax was probably the least adversely affected riding in the country. Without the VER, the entrance requirements in Halifax are 14 weeks and with it, they are 13.
Government Orders
Under the new legislation, they would have been 18. In the long run, without the VER, Halifax was not that much worse off. Ergo, I can enter this part of the debate, at least, with my halo shining. But I am thinking of other Atlantic Canadians. I am thinking of Cape Bretoners, and those from South West Nova and New Brunswick who were adversely affected by the absence of the VER.
I close by reminding the House that we on this side brought in the motion and agreed that we would bring it through without debate and this government voted it down. This is something that Atlantic Canadians will remember. They will remember it along with the theory that they do not want to work and that they are still sitting on the wharf whittling and waiting for the cheques to come in. They will remember for a long, long time.

I call upon the government to urge AECL to present our concerns for human rights in its negotiations with South Korea and make this commitment known to the House.
If Canada wants to maintain its reputation as an advocate of human rights, we cannot allow it to support through aid or trade authoritarian regimes, dictatorships and other violators of human rights.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House a unique tree planting ceremony which took place last Friday on the grounds of Government House.
Forestry Canada researchers achieved a major breakthrough in forest biotechnology, producing trees from a single cell culture. This allows for an unlimited number of trees from superior seeds to be bred for special characteristics, characteristics that will give improved growth, improved resistance to disease and to insects.
This is not only a major accomplishment by the government but it has good commercial applications. It is an example of what we in Canada can do. In National Forest Week it is one that I want to praise.

speakerposition: subtopic
Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, anyone who takes the government at its word on spending restraint had their eyes opened a little wider this weekend.
May 8, 1990

A newspaper report showed that Tory appointees at Ports Canada are living high on the hog-and I do mean hog. From sumptuous lunches at exclusive clubs to, dare I say, a Liberal approach to expense accounts, Port Canada executives are on a spending spree that would do Donald Trump justice.
Perhaps they are just following the proud example of restraint showed by salaries in the Prime Minister's office or at the Bank of Canada.
I would like to see the Minister of Transport explain it to people in my riding who have lost VIA Rail service because the government says it cannot afford it. I would like to see him explain it to the small businesses facing the GST because the government says it wants to bring the deficit down. I would like to see him deny that what the government really means by restraint is cut-backs for the rest of us while the Gucci crowd keeps raking it in.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today, May 8, World Red Cross Day will be celebrated in 149 countries throughout the world. One hundred and sixty-two years ago today Henry Dunant of Switzerland founded a movement which has made the world a better place for everyone. This movement, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent, has devoted itself to his ideal, namely, that the life of every human being must be respected and protected against the ravages of man and nature.
Respect for every human being, especially those in need, guides the efforts of the Red Cross and the Red Crescent. It helps those trapped in solitude or anguish. It helps those waiting in refugee camps, in hospitals or in prisons. Those who have seen their homes destroyed and the loss of everything dear to them depend on the help of the Red Cross. From the drought-stricken fields of Africa to the war zones of Southeast Asia the Red Cross provides humanitarian assistance where it is needed.
Canada recognizes the work of the Canadian Red Cross Society and supports the ideals for which it strives. Its many services make Canada a better place and help show Canada's humanity in alleviating the suffering of those in other countries.
Let us observe World Red Cross Day by taking time to reflect on the unceasing need to protect human life and dignity, not only of Canadians, but of all humanity.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, May 6 to 12 is National Forest Week-to encourage greater public awareness of the forest resource.
Formerly called Forest Fire Prevention Week, the new title reflects the many human and environmental needs Canada's forests are now expected to satisfy.
This week, the Canadian Forestry Association challenges all Canadians to learn more about Canada's forests and to think about the multitude of benefits derived from their wise management.
An aware and knowledgeable public is necessary to provide comprehensive conservation and management of one of Canada's greatest assets.
An aware and responsible federal government is also indispensable. I therefore urge this government to develop a sound environmental policy which will allow us to both properly utilize and protect our forest reserves.
The role the forests play nationally and, indeed, globally is of paramount importance to the continuing survival and economic and social prosperity of the citizens of the world.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this week across the country we are celebrating National Forest Week. Our forests are the backbone of this country's economy. They are the greatest of our natural resources.
Allow me to tell you, Madam Speaker, that no one knows the value of the forest better than the residents of Temagami.
I am not talking about the sightseers who travel for a day to view the pine stands of the area. I am talking about those former sawmill workers and the many foresters of the Timiskaming region. I am speaking about the many who have lived within the forests, respecting the sustained growth for generations, those individuals and families who once lived from the productive activi-

May 8, 1990
Oral Questions
ties of the forests and who can no longer gain access to them.
During National Forest Week we should reflect upon the fate of these Temagami families and take the time to consider the great value of working forests.
Multiple land use policies have enabled many Canadians throughout our history to enjoy a rich heritage of harvesting our country's greatest resource. I ask Canadians during this week to reflect and come to respect this heritage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Lithuanian MP in charge of internal security, Zigmas Vaisvila, has been hospitalized following a severe beating by Soviet troops. He went to the press building in Vilnius on April 20 to negotiate a peaceful settlement to the occupation of that building. After presenting his documents, a Colonel Fiodorov issued an order to club him. He sustained injury to his lungs, intestines and has sustained a contusion in the brain.
That deputy was presented to this House in late 1989.1 would urge colleagues and Canadians generally to send letters of support to him in care of the Supreme Council of Lithuania in Vilnius in a gesture of good will. I would urge our Secretary of State for External Affairs to issue a statement to the Soviet government protesting this action.
Finally, the Canadian delegation at the International Conference monitoring Helsinki Accords on the Human Dimension should bring this matter and all other human rights abuses in Lithuania to the attention of the conference.
