speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the premiers of the four western provinces gave a highly damaging assessment of this government's economic policies. In a joint communique they said, and I quote:
There is a growing crisis of confidence in the federal government's management of the Canadian economy, and current federal fiscal and monetary policies have created the real danger of a Made-in-Canada recession.
When will the government listen to the four western premiers, three of whom are members of the Prime Minister's own party, and stop these policies that are creating a made-in-Canada recession? Why does this government insist on creating a made-in-Canada recession?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unless something happened over the weekend there are only two premiers of my party out there, not three. But I will take that as a representation, officially.
You've left out Filmon, have you? Gary is gone!
They all voted against the GST-kick out all three.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
He says that they are all against the GST. We will have to see. Maybe we will have none at that point in time.
I read the comments of the western premiers, and I read the comments of the Premier of Newfoundland in regard to another matter. Clearly, you would have difficulty in getting unanimity in regard to an opinion on the Canadian economy from the provincial premiers. They all feel quite badly done by these days.
That is not the opinion of the World Economic Outlook provided by the IMF over the weekend. For Canada, it stated:
Continuation of the present monetary policy would seem appropriate until there are convincing signs that inflationary pressures are abating.
It went on to state:
A number of important structural initiatives are under way in Canada, including reforms relating to the sales tax and the unemployment insurance system. Together with previous tax reform measures and with the implementation of the Free Trade Agreement with the United States, these initiatives should significantly improve the efficiency of the economy and enhance growth prospects.
May 8, 1990

I realize that all provinces and all premiers have matters that concern them greatly, and we are seeking as best we can to respond to the concerns.
The Minister of Agriculture put out a $500 million package most recently to assist the western farmers. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has just come back from an almost $600 million dollar investment on behalf of the people of Canada in the fishery of Atlantic Canada.
While there are difficulties everywhere, it is interesting to note that the IMF has pointed out that the Government of Canada in difficult times is pursuing economic, fiscal and monetary policies that, while somewhat painful and difficult for the moment for many Canadians, will turn out to be precisely the prescriptions that the Canadian economy requires to provide for a period of sustained, non-inflationary economic growth, which is what Canadians require.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the people of western Canada and Canada as a whole would prefer that the Prime Minister listen to people in this country, in this case the four western premiers, rather than the International Monetary Fund. I know that the Prime Minister would like them to disappear, but the last time I looked there were three Conservative premiers: Filmon, Devine and Getty. I am not sure which one he would like to get rid of, but I know-
Hear, hear!
All three.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I know the Deputy Prime Minister's close friend and fellow Albertan, Premier Don Getty-and maybe that is the one that the Prime Minister wants to get rid of-said that in their obsession with inflation federal officials "are fighting an imaginary foe while they drive us into a shuddering halt with our economy".
So far the government has offered even less to western farmers this year than the totally inadequate package it offered to the Atlantic fishery yesterday, the package that has been rejected almost unanimously by the people of Atlantic Canada.
For example, the mayor of Trepassey, Rita Pennell, said: "They talk about rebuilding the stocks, but they're rebuilding the stocks for the large companies-certainly
Oral Questions
not rebuilding for people. What we need is something to tide us over until the stocks rebuild".
Why did the government not offer a realistic program for the recovery of the Atlantic fishery? Is it because this government feared reprisals from the United States under the free trade deal that offered so limited, so constrained a program for the recovery of the Atlantic fishery?
If this is not the case, why did the government not offer a meaningful program for the preservation of Atlantic communities and the fishery until the fishery stocks of Atlantic Canada were rebuilt? Is it not fear of reprisal under the trade deal that made this government offer such a totally inadequate program to the people of Atlantic Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize to my hon. friend. I did not hear an important part of the preface of his first question about the Conservative premiers. In point of fact there are so many of them around, they are hard to keep track of.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!
They're going off in all directions.
They're an endangered species.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot help.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, few people can. Obviously, we embrace all Conservative provincial premiers with equal affection. I would not want to convey any other impression.
With regard to the announcement made yesterday by my hon. friend, the Minister of Fisheries, I would have thought that the Leader of the Opposition would have, while not being in full agreement with everything, pointed out a number of the very beneficial aspects of this important program for the benefit of Atlantic fishermen.
It is almost a $600 million package. It deals with some of the very important structural problems that have afflicted the fishery. It deals with conservation. It deals with community futures. It deals with retraining. It deals with a lot of the important fundamentals.
Unfortunately, it does not and cannot by itself bring the fish back tomorrow to ensure that everybody in Atlantic Canada who wishes to can have a substantial job out of the fishery. But it does deal with some of the

May 8, 1990
Oral Questions
fundamental problems that have been long neglected and overdue for action by the Government of Canada.
One of the things that has been carefully considered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this is the increased vigilance with which the Government of Canada will deal with all foreigners who seek to fish off our coasts and ensure that all their activities are in full and rigid compliance with international law.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is what the Conservative Member for Gaspe thinks about the program announced by the federal fisheries minister, and I quote: "There is nothing for Quebec in the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program". Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Gaspe, who is chairman of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans, added that the funds allocated to Quebec were peanut. I therefore would like to ask the Prime Minister why the government is treating Quebec's fishermen so unfairly. Why are the fishermen of this province getting this offhand treatment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member keeps telling us what other people think. He might let us know what he thinks. If he took the trouble to examine the adjustment program announced yesterday, he would realize that the program contains several components that will benefit fishermen and communities along the coast of Quebec.
For the information of the hon. member and the House, if they are interested, I have already started talks with my provincial counterpart, Minister Page. In fact, we are supposed to meet this Friday to discuss further measures that could be taken jointly with the Government of Quebec for the benefit of maritime Quebec.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government announced yesterday: "No more groundfish licences will be issued to fishermen in
Newfoundland and Labrador", and that "fishing should be regarded as a skilled profession requiring a range of technical and managerial skills. We propose a formal training apprenticeship and certification program for fishermen".
My question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Does this licence cut-off now mean that a young man or young woman who just started fishing with their father or a relative in the fishing boat, or will start fishing this summer, will not be able to get a groundfish licence, ending the fishing tradition in that family?
What happens if the full-time fisherman who has not been near a classroom for decades flunks this formal training apprenticeship and certification program?
It is not the fishermen who need training, it is this minister and his officials who need the training.
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, I am not surprised, given the record of that party while it was in power, that it is looking at fishermen as people who have no qualifications, people who have nothing except to go out there and fish.
We believe in the fishermen of Atlantic Canada. We believe in the fishermen of Newfoundland. This suggestion for the professionalization and certification project was made to this government by the fishermen in his backyard, in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Mr. Speaker, the fishermen of Newfoundland and Labrador think that this program is an insult.
In order to add insult to injury, the Minister of Fisheries announces a lot of money now to try to find out what seals eat. Well, Mr. Speaker, the fishermen have told him what seals eat, and it ain't turnips.
Why did the minister announce yesterday: "Canadians have had difficulty locating and catching commercial quantities of turbot in the northern waters, 2J and 3K, even though Soviet and other East Bloc countries harvest these stocks on a regular basis"? Does the minister realize that we have harvested that stock for hundreds of years before the Soviets even knew what a boat looked like?
May 8, 1990

Why is the minister issuing these foreign licences for that zone in this year for Canadian quotas of turbot and codfish while Newfoundlanders are being chased out of their boats?
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, it is easy to come into this House and grandstand on the issue of foreign overfishing.
Oh, oh!
Look who's talking. Sit down!
Your halo is slipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they do not want to hear the answer. When they are totally devoid of ideas they just shout you down. But it will not work with this guy here.
With respect to foreign overfishing, I am going to tell the hon. member and every member in this House that if there are fishermen in Atlantic Canada, in all of Canada, who want to take every fish that can be caught under our quotas in the Canadian zone, then they can go out there and I will not allow one foreign boat to fish in Canada if our people want that.
He should have been with me yesterday when this gentleman, a colleague of his from P.E.I. was saying: "Go fish underutilized stock". The guy said: "I will not fish for six-cents-a-pound fish because I have got to buy fuel. I have got to pay labour. It is not viable".
I am telling the hon. member that if he wants fishing to take place, then support this program. We have a lot of stuff in there for underutilized stock. Support the program. You will help the fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, as the Prime Minister knows, the western premiers again said that the high interest rates are savaging the prairies. Premier Grant Devine said that to get lower interest rates he would be willing to see the dollar drop. In fact that is exactly what the Prime Minister said in 1984. When he was asked if he had to
Oral Questions
choose between high interest rates and a lower dollar he said: "I will take the lower dollar".
The Prime Minister knows that high interest rates in the west have cost Canadian farmers $330 million this year. They have pushed western farm bankruptcies up 22 per cent. They have threatened 10,000 Saskatchewan farmers with foreclosure and are pricing our farm products out of the world market.
Can the Prime Minister give us one positive effect of this high interest rate policy on Canadian farmers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the high interest rates, generally speaking, do not provide immediate, palpable and demonstrable benefits for ordinary hard working people. There is no secret in that. What high interest rates from time to time are required to do is to squeeze the inflation out of an economy because the inflation can cripple once and for all hard working ordinary Canadian citizens. Inflation is a pernicious evil that we cannot unleash on the Canadian economy.
The Liberals and the NDP conspired in the late seventies and early eighties to adopt a policy that allowed inflation to get out of hand. Unemployment sky-rocketed and the country economically just about became a basket case. We want to make sure that does not happen again so we are pursuing a policy that most of the international agencies, most recently the IMF, view as productive and important and necessary in the national interest.
The ultimate benefit of the monetary policy of Canada will be economic growth without damaging inflation to any serious extent. That is what we are pursuing and that policy will throw off benefits to farmers, fishermen, auto workers and all Canadians alike.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is to the Prime Minister.
The question that farmers have and that fishermen have on the east coast is what is going to be left for them. If we look at the farm income projected for this year, the farm income is supposed to go down 63 per cent on the prairies. It is supposed to go down 87 per cent in Saskatchewan and 46 per cent in Alberta.
The Prime Minister's government has promised assistance for western farmers; it has promised $500 million. The government knows that the provinces in the west with declining farm incomes cannot afford to match that

May 8, 1990
Oral Questions
assistance. When you offer something to these provinces that they cannot possibly accept, it is no offer at all.
Will the federal government now drop its conditions to the provinces and give the assistance to Canadian farmers that they need right now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government offered to provide $500 million worth of assistance to the farmers in Canada.
We are strapped for financial resources. We are limited. We asked the provinces to assist us in developing a kind of package that would put more money into the hands of farmers. If the provinces absolutely refuse to participate, it will obviously mean that there will be less money to be distributed to the farmers.
We are really trying to develop the kind of package that the provinces want some share in the responsibility of. They want a kind of package that would zero in on the problems of each of the respective provinces because it is a multifaceted problem. It is drought in some areas. It is the impact of interest rates. It is the impact of low prices. It is a variation of things.
We have simply said that we are prepared to sit down and work with them in developing a plan that will improve the incomes of farmers for 1990. If they absolutely refuse to participate in that process, it will mean that there will be less money to be distributed. I regret that. As a matter of fact I am somewhat saddened by the fact that they would rather play politics than really help the farmers. That is what we intend to do, and that is our bottom line.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. Those 10,000 Saskatchewan farmers are not playing politics; they are just trying to survive.
This government is tying conditions that cannot be met to funding and assistance to farmers. After all, it is this government's constitutional responsibility to ensure that the interests of Canadian agriculture are protected in international trade. Expecting prairie provinces that have declining income, 63 per cent this year, to match
assistance dollar for dollar is like asking a drowning man to throw himself a line.
I ask the minister again: Are the prairies going to sink or swim? Will the government live up to its constitutional responsibility to Canadian farmers and do it now before farmers drown?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party engaged in a typical NDP distortion.
I was not accusing the farmers of playing politics. I was simply attempting to answer the question and outline our strategy for getting the greatest amount of money into the hands of the farmers. That can best be achieved with the support and co-operation of the provinces. If that is not forthcoming, obviously we will have to look at another alternative.
We are not here to play politics with the farmers' welfare, but we really regret very much that the premiers of the provinces are not prepared to share in their responsibility.
After all, this government has been providing up to 90 per cent plus in terms of support for agriculture in western Canada. We think it is time the provinces paid their fair share.

Mr. Speaker, I want to pose a question of the same minister and preface it by saying that even though some of them may have been dropped from the Christmas card list of the Prime Minister, I do not think he is being fair to them.
If I may, I want to simply quote from the communique: "The western premiers note that the 1990 income deficiency is a direct result of international trade subsidy wars and as such must be addressed by the federal government". They go on to point out that the United States government is now providing over $1 more support for a bushel of grain than the Canadian government provides to try to beat western Canadian farmers out of the international market.
Under those circumstances is it not proper and responsible for this national government to match at least the efforts of other governments to keep western farmers in
May 8, 1990

business, keep the grain economy going and not let the Europeans and Americans push us out of our rightful grain market that we have had for the last 50 years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take from the hon. member that that is a representation asking the federal government to put in place a contingency fund as the premiers have asked.
If that is what the hon. member is asking for, I will take that as a representation. If he is suggesting that we put the $500 million into a form of contingency fund to fight the international price war, I will take that under serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the question I am posing is not just in respect of a contingency fund.
It is a comprehensive agricultural program which meets the international support subsidies that come from the Americans and the Europeans. It is one that will bring down interest rates so that 30 per cent of farmers who are now facing bankruptcy will not go broke. It is a program that will deal with the major problem of soil erosion and the major loss of markets.
When is this government going to come up with a comprehensive agricultural program so that western Canada will not face not only a recession but the depression which it is now facing straight on because of this government's lack of attention to its interest and its problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was merely trying to extract from the hon. member what sort of policy position he would follow, because we know what he did when he was on the government side and interest rates went to 24 per cent. They did absolutely nothing.
I have the communique that says western premiers call upon the federal government either to raise initial grain prices or set a $1 billion contingency fund to offset future impacts of the U.S. and European subsidies.
If that is the position of the hon. member, I indicated to him that I would give it serious consideration. We have $500 million. We asked the provinces to sit down and design a program involving some sharing on their
Oral Questions
part so that we could get money into the hands of farmers now.
The hon. member is suggesting that we put this money aside in a contingency fund to fight the international price wars. If that is his recommendation, I will give it serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture who I hope will listen to some reason.
The federal government has offered $500 million in farm aid. Farmers desperately need that money because they have been badly hurt by the international subsidy war, high interest rates, the high dollar value, low grain prices, and drought. All these problems are beyond provincial control, yet the federal government will not make good on its offer unless the provinces participate.
Why? The federal government has the money; the farmers need the money. Why not release it now without any strings attached so that there will be no more damage to farmers and their families?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The answer to that question, Mr. Speaker, is very simple.
Quite obviously what I was trying to achieve was $1 billion distributed to the hands of the farmers rather than $500 million. I thought that with the provinces' generosity and their co-operation we could have put $1 billion into the hands of the farmers.
I understand that this member is interested in getting only $500 million out to the farmers and does not care about the rest.

Mr. Speaker, I point out that over and over again the minister has insisted that the provinces match the federal offer dollar for dollar.
Yet, just this morning in the Winnipeg Free Press the Minister of Agriculture is quoted as saying that if the Manitoba government comes through with $8 million, the federal government will come through with a contribution of $63 million.
I want to know what is going on. Is this a new set of conditions? What kind of game is this minister playing with the farmers of Canada? Why not just release the

May 8, 1990
Oral Questions
money now, no strings attached, as insisted upon by the western premiers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the hon. member does not follow the debate more closely but rather gets engaged in his own rhetoric.
I indicated in the House yesterday that the Manitoba government had come up with programs which would be eligible for a matching contribution from the federal government. We are at the stage now where $8 million from the provincial government would generate a payout of about $72 million to the farmers in Manitoba. I think that is a pretty good deal for the farmers and for the Government of Manitoba.
I would urge the hon. member to use his good office to influence the Government of Manitoba to come on board. I think this could facilitate and speed up the process very much.
In commenting, the hon. member should know that since this government came into office support to the agricultural sector, particularly to western Canada, has increased by about 600 per cent over the time the party of which he is a member was in office.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Yesterday the minister admitted that some rejected refugee claimants have been drugged against their will so they could be easily transported from Canada. This practice directly contravenes the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Canada has no statutory justification for the compulsory sedation of detainees. It is not even used on convicted criminals who are being transported on commercial airlines.
My question to the minister is: Will she table in the House a list of the deportees who have been drugged against their will since January 1, 1989? Will she make public the existing departmental guidelines under which this practice has been condoned?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the question and the preamble to it were distorted from what was actually said.
I want to make the facts very clear because I know the hon. member has an interest in this issue. I want to take the time to explain thoroughly.
First, deportations come at the end of a long legal process after avenues of appeal on humanitarian and compassionate grounds have been considered. From January 1, 1989 until currently there have been 3,125 deportations from Canada of which 9 came following some medical examination. If someone who is to be deported and in the eyes of an immigration official requires medical treatment of any sort whether it is because they are diabetic or have a heart condition, they then call in a medical examiner. So, the 9 of the 3,125 could have been examined for any reason.
If that medical examiner determines that some medication is required, it is the medical examiner who administers that treatment whatever it may be.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered my question at all and I regret that she is refusing to put the facts on the table. She must be aware that the charter of Canada says that everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
Will she put a halt to the practice of compelling deportees to be drugged in certain cases against their will, or at least suspend that practice until it can be reviewed. In other words, will the minister just say 'no' to drugs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tried to outline that there are some safety considerations involved. We have had an immigration officer who was injured in the process of accompanying a deportee travelling back to another country. Whatever treatment is to be administered is determined by a medical examiner, a doctor. It is not determined by myself. It is between the doctor and the person being examined. It is for the courts to decide if there is a complaint under the charter. It is not up to me to interfere with medical practice under the laws of a province in which the law is administered by a medical examiner.
May 8, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. Yesterday the minister not only condoned but defended the drugging of deportees against their own free will.
I have confirmed with two previous Liberal ministers of immigration that this clearly was not a policy of those previous administrations.
Therefore I ask the minister whether she can now clarify if this offensive practice represents an official policy of this government and please inform the House why this became policy when in fact before, when we were still deporting people, this practice was not only not condoned but was not utilized and other means respecting medical, ethical, and human rights codes were utilized?
Is this policy, when was it started, and why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to indicate to the House and to the hon. member that it is not a policy of this government. I would certainly be disappointed to learn that prior ministers of immigration did not call for medical assistance to treat people who are to be deported if such is necessary.
That is the action we take. Any treatment from there on is between the medical examiner and the person involved.

Mr. Speaker, I find it ironic that refugees flee countries whose regimes have no respect for human rights and this government then deports people by flagrantly abusing another aspect of those same human rights. The minister cannot have it both ways.
I ask the minister again, after having reflected on this serious issue, is the minister now prepared to put an immediate end to such a deplorable practice? Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate today in support of the motion of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
We have to go back a little in history to take a clear look at what we are doing as a party and what we are attempting to do with Bill C-21.
In the Throne Speech last year, we set out our intention to build a strong economy. We intended to put Bill C-21 into that sense of building a strong economy and building an economy that responds to the needs of the 1990s and into the year 2000.
The reason we are going in this direction is quite simply this. In 1984, when we took office, we made a commitment to the Canadian people that we were going to take the country in a direction that had been missing for many years under previous administrations. We in fact did that. In checking the record of what we had done between 1984 and 1988, Canada has had the strongest economy in the world. Between 1984 and 1988, we ranked number two in terms of growth in the world behind just one country, Japan. That clearly illustrates that we are doing the right things, going in the right direction, and doing the things that Canadians elected us to do.
This holds true for Bill C-21. We were elected in 1988 to do the right things and to do the things that would put Canada number one in the world in relation to growth, our ability to do things for ourselves, and training for workers. That is exactly what Bill C-21 is all about. It is to thrust us into the 21st century in a way which was not possible under the old administration. That, in a sense, is the history of that party.
I cannot talk in that sense about the NDP party, because, fortunately for Canadians, it has never formed a government in the country and God forbid that it ever would.

Not one member of the House on the opposition side, whether they be NDP or Liberal, stood up and gave us one ounce of credit for what we did yesterday, not one ounce. Why? speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure what it is about this member of Parliament, but every time I get up to speak I am rudely interrupted by the opposition. I am not sure if it is because of where I am placed strategically in this House, but every time I speak I am always the focus of a great deal of criticism from that side of the House. I can take the criticism that they are levying at me because it is simply a reaction going back to those years, as I mentioned before I sat down, of that $200 billion debt with which they saddled us.
Before I sat down, I was mentioning the fishing aid package announced yesterday and the fact that there was not a positive statement from those people on that side of the House in relation to that package. I expect absolutely nothing positive from that particular party.
Returning to the bill we are debating today, the proposals that they are putting forward to Bill C-21 simply, clearly, and undeniably point in the direction that that party has taken for many, many years.
They are putting in proposals, via the Senate, that will raise the cost of that bill by $1.7 billion. The point that I
May 8, 1990

am making is that historically the only way they get out from underneath a problem is simply by buying their way out.
In Canada, we have developed programs to help Canadians. There is no question about that. We are very proud of the safety nets that we have developed for the Canadian people, for example, for senior citizens who receive old age pension cheques, Canada pension, and the best health care in the world. We are very proud of those social nets. Those are the kinds of social programs that we want to continue to create in Canada. Most importantly, we want to create programs that we can actually pay for.
The difference between us and the socialist parties, and the Liberal party most notably, is that they want to take those safety nets and use them to entrap Canadians. Instead of using those nets as they are intended, to help and protect people, they want to entrap Canadians in them.
It is pretty clear, Madam Speaker, if you read Bill C-21, that that is exactly what they are attempting to do. No one who is knowledgeable about education and training workers would object to what we are attempting to do in Bill C-21. We want to train Canadians for the future. The opposition is living in a dream world. They are dreaming in technicolour. We are living in a world that is very competitive, where competition is not the province next door or the community next door, it is the world. If we have fallen down as Canadians, that is where we have fallen down.
There is not a member in the House who could dispute the fact that we are competing with the big world. Those workers in Canada who find themselves displaced from the workforce deserve something more than just simply money, a cheque. A cheque does nothing at all to solve that problem.
The Liberal party and the NDP do not want to face that reality. They do not want to open up that door at all. They just simply want to hand out money, regardless of whether or not we have it, just sign the cheque and get it out. To heck with the real problem, do not address the root of the problem, just throw money at it. We are not going to do that.
I want to take the liberty to point out some statistics to our friends on the other side. Bill C-21 allows for a 45
Government Orders
per cent increase in funding for labour force development. It will give life to the Labour Lorce Development Strategy; a 45 per cent increase. Does that indicate to you, Madam Speaker, that we are on the right track? I think it does. It will increase the quantity of training and of skills for workers, and with a greater commitment on the part of the private sector. That is an area in which we have fallen down drastically in this country.
We as a nation spend less than one-half the amount that U.S. firms spend on training. That tells us something about being competitive in the market-place. What the U.S. spends on training is just a fraction of what other countries like Japan spend for their workers.
Bill C-21 will commit $231 million to training in the private sector. That money will be leveraged with private funding. That will bring in about something in the order of $1.5 billion in additional investment for training in that sector.
Our goal is to create a training culture where employees and companies practice development skills on an ongoing basis so that we can remain competitive in that real world, and that we are not afraid to address it as a government and I do not think we are afraid to address it as a nation.
Part and parcel of Bill C-21 is $100 million for the purpose of setting up new entry level training programs directed at young people. If we are going to have a future and if this country is going to enjoy prosperity in the coming years, it has to be through the young people who are replacing us in the workforce. We have to offer them the training that they need to get out there and compete, whether it be at the university level or the technical school level. We must do it. We are putting dollars into programs to make sure that that happens.
I am not sure why, but in my province of New Brunswick, there is a high degree of illiteracy in Atlantic Canada. In fact, the educational levels of Canadians increase from east to west. It might have to do with the fact that many of our trained and educated workers have had to move from Atlantic Canada to other parts of the country. Maybe there is an equation there of some sort or correlation between those statistics.
There is no question that there is a high degree of illiteracy in my home province of New Brunswick. The same holds true in Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. It improves somewhat moving through Quebec and Ontario. British Columbia has the statistic

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
which we are attempting to achieve back in New Brunswick. It has the lowest rate of illiteracy in the country.
There is no question that the success of our province and of Atlantic Canada hinges on legislation like Bill C-21, because it is going to address some of those very real problems that we cannot duck. We cannot duck those problems in the real world.
We can stand here in this House and criticize every single bill that comes before this House, if we want to be nitpicking because no bill is ever perfect. We are all mortals in this House, Madam Speaker, and we are attempting to deal with problems brought on by Canadians like you and I and we are not going to solve those problems by running and hiding from them.
Unemployed workers will receive an additional $350 million under this program. That will reach 60,000 additional UI claimants in the country. Another $50 million will go to current training employment programs in co-operation with the provinces, and we have done that since 1986.
The problem with this particular bill is that it is being held up in the Senate. The Senators are doing it for a very simple reason.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Because the bill is no good.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Partisan reasons. They can claim the bill is no good, but they have to prove that it is no good and they cannot do it. They have not done it yet and they will not do it. They can get up on their hind legs and cry and holler and wave their arms, but the truth is they do not have a realistic alternative to this bill.
Let me read some of the editorials from around the country concerning this bill and what they have had to say about it: "The arrogance" they call it "of the unelected Senate". We have to remember that the opposition in this House, namely the Liberal party, are taking their marching orders from Allan. We refer to him as Uncle Allan in the Senate. That is who gives the marching orders. It is not the whip or the House leader. It is their leader in the Senate.
I want to quote what Mr. MacEachen had to say about the Senate as he was being sworn in as a Senator. As you know, Madam Speaker, it was Prime Minister Trudeau who put Mr. MacEachen in the Senate. This is what Mr. MacEachen had to say about the Senate when he was appointed back in 1984:
No member of this chamber would suggest that the Senate should-systematically obstruct the will of the majority in the elected body of Parliament-
That is what he said. He is not a man of his word, because he has pulled this trick on the House of Commons on a number of occasions going right back to the election of 1988 and our free trade agreement.
There is a connection between this bill, the free trade agreement and the GST. The theme that I have been trying to reach in my short time is simply that we are part of a very competitive world. The UI bill will make us more competitive. The incentive is to get further training, to get into the industries and the areas of technology that we have to enter. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to rise today in the debate on the government's motion moved by the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
I am especially delighted that I am able to speak on the amendment to that motion proposed by my hon. colleague from Saskatoon-Dundum which would basically thank the Senate for its interesting work and simply withdraw the bill, because that is the fate it most definitely warrants.
Before addressing particularly the merits of the government's motion and the amendment before us, I would like briefly to review the highlights, if that term can reasonably be applied here, of the history and contents of Bill C-21 as we now have it. To start, we must bear in mind throughout the entirety of this discussion that the Mulroney government's changes to the unemployment insurance program are a major part of a fundamental shift in the way income security programs are designed and financed in Canada.
These changes to unemployment insurance are an attack on both the employed and the unemployed. They will have the effect of moving our UI system closer to the American model of which this government seems so enamoured in so many realms.
Despite all the changes made to UI since it was introduced in 1940, many of its fundamental principles- thus far-remain intact. Unemployment insurance is a social insurance program designed to replace workers' earnings during an interruption of earnings due to job loss, or leave due to pregnancy, sickness, child care or training. The burden of funding is split among workers, employers and the federal government, thus far.
It must be emphasized that UI is not a social assistance program. It is not designed to redistribute wealth from the well-to-do to the less-well-off. Such assistance programs as the social allowance, the guaranteed income supplement and, should we ever achieve it, a guaranteed annual income, are designed to protect people against absolute deprivation.


May 8, 1990

By contrast, UI is a social insurance program which, like the Canada Pension Plan and Workers' Compensation, is designed to replace earnings in the event of unemployment, just as the others are designed to replace earnings in the event of retirement or an accident in the workplace, respectively.
UI is a program that benefits most Canadians. While it is easy for us who have actually been unemployed to see the value of UI, it is equally certain that UI benefits those who remain employed. As the Alberta Federation of Labour put it in their excellent brief to the UI legislative committee in Edmonton on September 13:
The income security provided by UI allows employed workers to consume more of what they earn, and hence enjoy a higher standard of living, than would be the case if they had to hedge their consumption patterns against the risk of unemployment.
So unemployment insurance is an integral part of that collection of Canadian social programs that sets us apart fundamentally from, for example, our less fortunate neighbours to the south. In Canada we recognize the value of co-operative collective efforts to insure ourselves and our friends and neighbours against hard times, and we do so through our governments.
But the Mulroney government is setting about to change this, in part through this bill. How?
First, Bill C-21 will cut regular UI benefits by more than $1.5 billion a year. It will do this in three ways. First, it will do it by increasing the entrance requirements from 10 to 14 weeks of work to 10 to 20 weeks of work, with many more instances of 20 weeks being required. Second, it will reduce the maximum duration of benefits. Third, it will increase the penalties on UI claimants who quit or are fired from their jobs from the current maximum of six weeks penalty to a minimum of seven weeks and a maximum of 12 weeks penalty.
Second, Madam Speaker, Bill C-21 will transfer the government's entire share of UI benefit costs-about $2 billion a year-to workers and employers. This is a complete rejection of the current recognition of the effect government policy has on unemployment rates. Under existing UI legislation the government's share includes regionally extended benefits when the local unemployment rate is over 4 per cent.
Government Orders
Third, the government will allow the UI Commission to use up to 15 per cent of UI funds for schemes and programs such as training, work sharing, job creation, moving costs, travel, business start-up, self-employment bonuses to accept a job quickly, and so on. This means that job training programs will be paid for, not out of general revenue as is currently the case but out of funds snatched from the existing UI safety net.
In all these ways the government is cutting unemployment insurance. How will these changes affect working Canadians? The most obvious effect will be that workers will have less protection against catastrophic income loss when thrown out of work.
In its release of October 2 the Canadian Council on Social Development stated: "The government is performing a high wire act with the income security of Canadians in the balance". By making UI harder to get, the government is in a sense taking one of Canada's most important safety nets out from under that high wire and moving it further and further away.
According to Statistics Canada figures obtained by the Canadian Labour Congress, increasing the number of weeks of work required to be eligible for benefits-and this is only one aspect of the changes-alone would have meant that nearly 130,000 Canadians who received benefits last year would not have received those benefits.
In Alberta, 5,400 UI claimants would have lost their benefits. In Edmonton alone, 3,000 people, accounting for $12 million in benefits, would not have qualified for UI.
The massive cuts in UI benefits will also increase the power of employers over workers. Unemployed workers denied benefits will naturally be more inclined to take the first job open to them, regardless of the wages and benefits paid by that job, and those with jobs will have fewer options and will be forced to put up with harassment or with unsatisfactory, low paid, and even unsafe work.
The erosion of UI thus not only diminishes the protection of workers who lose their jobs. It also tends to erode the wages and working conditions of all workers by providing employers with a greater opportunity to take advantage of the desperation of the unemployed and the underemployed.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
In classic economic terms this is called disciplining the working class. It is odious and contemptible. Even when they are employed, workers will be hit directly in the pocket book. Starting January 1 of this year premiums will have risen by 15 per cent costing a worker making by a no means princely $400 a week an extra $62.40 a year.
It gets worse yet. Another effect will be equally foul. Those workers who need UI the most will be the hardest hit by the cuts. According to a Global Economics study, 80 per cent of all Canadians negatively affected will have annual incomes under $25,000 a year.
In Alberta, 72 per cent of those harmed by the changes, that is 51,000 people, will have an income of less than $20,000 a year. A full 32 per cent, or 23,000 people, will have incomes below $10,000 a year and will experience an average reduction in benefits of $1,800, fully 18 per cent of that meagre $10,000 a year. As incredible as it may seem, this bosses' government is proposing to enrich itself by further impoverishing those earning only $10,000 a year.
Why is the government doing this? We keep hearing the same refrain: "The deficit made us do it". Yet the Mulroney government persists in letting 60,000 profitable corporations pay no income tax at all, and more than 6,000 Canadians earning more than $50,000 a year continue to pay not a penny in personal income tax. By lowering the interest rate by 2 per cent, which it doggedly refuses to do, it could reduce that Satanic deficit by $3.5 billion. Let us hear no more about this phoney deficit justification. It does not wash. It is not the reason.
What is the reason, then? Perhaps, just maybe, these changes are intended to help put Canadian business on what the government loves to call a level playing field with business in the United States. Lord knows it is not level at the moment, at least not so far as UI is concerned. Here in Canada 83 per cent of unemployed workers collect UI. In the U.S. only 25 per cent do. In Canada UI pays out up to 60 per cent of workers' average weekly wages. In the U.S., UI pays just 35 per cent. In Canada the average duration of UI benefits is 22 weeks. In the U.S. it is less than 15 weeks.
That is the direction in which Bill C-21 starts to Jake us. We are not there yet, but that is the level playing field that big business boosters of free trade are pushing for.
The government is using the bulldozer of Bill C-21 to help start the levelling. Not only is doing so wrong on the face of it, it is also hypocritical. Do you remember, Madam Speaker, that before the last election the government promised Canadian workers worried about the effect of the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal that they would have one of the finest adjustment programs in the industrial world? Do you remember how on November 15, 1988, just six days before the election, the government reinforced this calming message by raising UI benefits and lowering premiums? It is true. Now, just over a year later, the trade deal is signed and the government is slashing UI benefits and jacking up premiums.
Cynical, opportunistic, savage and anti-Canadian, that is Bill C-21. But the government will have its way. Oh, yes, the government will have its way. Bill C-21 will pass in this House and be rammed through the other place and become law and no member of this House, indeed no citizen of this country, is under any illusion in that regard. It may be wrong. It may be unjust. It may be cruel. It may even be a little touch of treason against the overwhelming majority of people whose Canada this really is, the people who go to work every day, day after day, for a wage or a salary, who seek to build a family and have a decent life for themselves. But that does not matter because the government will get what it wants.
This brings us back to the government motion before us and the amendment moved by my friend, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundurn. The amendments that the Senate has passed to us, while not without merit, are quite simply inadequate to deal with the fundamental execrable flaws in Bill C-21. Therefore, it matters little if the government picks and chooses among the amendments given to this House from the other place and decides that it may magnanimously adopt this little piece of tinkering here while having, unfortunately, to disregard that other little piece of tinkering there. All of that is immaterial when one considers the effects that Bill C-21 still will have on the vast majority of working people in this country.
May 8, 1990

It is not the government's motion that I wish to commend to the House today, but rather the amendment of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundurn. I urge every member in this House with ears to hear and a heart to feel and a brain to think, to accept that amendment, thank the Senate for its work, and have this bill withdrawn.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps we ought to remind ourselves that we are here once again with Bill C-21 entitled an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.
A little more graphically, the assignment of the House, although we on this side refuse to participate in it, is to gut absolutely and irrevocably a very good piece of legislation that has served this country very well for a very long time, since I believe about 1978. Bill C-21, if implemented, would have the effect of doing some very damaging things to the country and to many thousands of people.
I hope that the gentleman from Carleton-Charlotte will pay close attention to what I have to say. I listened with great interest to him, as well. I thought the highlight of his entire presentation was when he spared no effort in praising some great social programs; what he called, and rightly so, the social net. He talked about medicare. He talked, by inference, about unemployment insurance. He mentioned the Canada Pension Plan specifically and then later in his discourse he mentioned the whole question of student financial aid programs.
I like a man who is fair. I must say that I took a certain comfort from the words of the gentleman from Carle-ton-Charlotte because he was in the process calling to the attention of the House a number of great social programs, all of which without exception were legislated by Liberal governments over the past several years.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
My friend, the minister of energy, feels a speech coming on. We are looking forward to hearing from him in due course. In the meantime I would like to say to the gentleman from Carleton-Charlotte that I appreciated his citing those programs. He ought to have gone the extra step and pointed out two facts: one, that these programs were brought in by Liberal governments, and second: that the fight that we have had on Bill C-21 really characterizes what the larger fight is about.
We have been trying on this side since 1984 to stop the flood gates and to hold back the dikes because this Tory government, of which the member from Carleton- Charlotte is a supporter, is systematically dismantling and gutting those programs. I thought it significant that he should have spent some time talking about the student aid programs. I want to remind him that the students in universities and in post-secondary institutions in general are having much difficulty making ends meet financially these days because the government that he supports has refused since 1984 to change the basic financial guidelines.
It simply means that the students of 1990 who will be going to university this fall- some will not be going because of the policies of this government-will be asked to live on the same basic amount in terms of student loan assistance as their counterparts did six or seven years before. If he is concerned about that particular program maybe he should talk to his colleagues and see what they can do to stop socking it to those students in post-secondary institutions.
I rise to speak in this debate because I believe that the bill, if passed, will do some really terrible things to fishermen and their unemployment insurance. Of all the people who will be at risk by the passage of this legislation, none is more at risk than the fishermen. That is why the Senate took some time to propose a number of amendments.
The fishermen of this country are facing most desperate times, particularly in places like my riding of Burin- St. George's. It has 158 communities and there is hardly a one that does not have some direct involvement in the fishery. There is a total of 17,000 fishermen and plant
workers who make their living directly from the fishery in the riding of Burin-St. George's. Many of those 17,000 are fishermen, either trawlermen or what we call inshore or near-shore fishermen. They are those people who commute to the fishery each morning and back home each night in boats that are from 20 feet to 50 feet long and in some cases, up to 65 feet long.
This bill, if passed, would, to use the fishing term one more time, gut the program as it relates to fishermen. I use that term because it is graphic and it strikes a note with my good friend, the minister of energy. If we could only get him to reflect on this, go back to cabinet and tell his colleagues in cabinet that they are very wrong in wanting to jeopardize the fishermen's benefits. Let me give you an example, Madam Speaker.
In 1988 fishermen paid approximately $18 million into the unemployment insurance fund and they received $269 million in benefits. That is quite a gap. It was otherwise in prior years when we had a viable fishery. There are some times when the fishermen are paying in much less than they are drawing down. If the government is going to back out of the program completely, who is going to make up that difference which, in 1988, was a difference of $251 million? The fear, of course, is that eventually some politicians will make a decision that it is time to scrap the fishermen's program as it relates to unemployment insurance. Under this bill, the unemployment insurance benefits to fishermen could be revoked by the approval of the Governor in Council only, by a cabinet decision. It is blatantly wrong that any cabinet of any government, sitting around the cabinet table, with their own immediate political agenda, without reference to the built-in accountability of Parliament, should have the authority to wipe out the benefits of such a large group of people in this country.
I could go on to deal with the adverse impact on unemployment insurance for fishermen, but I believe the point is made that we have had a good piece of legislation as it relates to fishermen and this is no time to do away with it, when the Atlantic fishery is on its knees.
Yesterday, my friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs talked about the Atlantic fishery not being in jeopardy.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can inform the hon. member for Levis that on the contrary, I think it is very much to the point in this debate to draw the attention of the House to the motives of the Prime Minister.

It is absolutely important. It is crucial. It is related to the bill. If my friend from Levis really wants to understand why this piece of garbage called Bill C-21 is here, it is because the Prime Minister is marching to a very different drummer than the fishermen on the south coast of Newfoundland.
It also explains what the government is doing in terms of the closure of rural post offices. It explains what it is doing in terms of the goods and services tax. It explains what it is doing in terms of the so-called aid program for fishermen. It is aimed at the shutting down of rural Canada, whether that rural Canada fishes or farms.
This government has no interest in the geographic extremities of this country. This government has no interest in people who happen to draw average or below average incomes. How else can you explain the statistics? For those who earn $100,000 or more a year, federal income tax and other federal taxes have gone down by $1,600 a year since this Prime Minister took office in 1984. However, for those who earn $35,000 or less-and that covers every fisherman in my riding-federal taxes have gone up by $1,200 a year.
I understand that, for the hon. gentleman from Levis, it is a tender point when I get close to home on what the real motivation is of the Prime Minister, when I take his own words, and when I come to his defence and say: "No, the Prime Minister is absolutely right. He is not a masochist." Equally, I can say that he is a political terrorist and hijacker who has hijacked the people of the country, taking them where they do not want to go.
Eighty per cent of the people have said in polls: "We do not want a goods and services tax." Yet, it is being rammed down their throats. Why will the government not listen to the people who it is supposed to be serving?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the minister insists on being despicable, I shall attempt to refrain from responding in kind.
May 8, 1990

I want to talk about what another minister said. The Minister of Employment and Immigration who sponsors this bill made a great noise yesterday. She talked about how she could not respond to the Message from the Senate because, in her words, it would infringe on the privilege of the House of Commons to implement money bills.
I do not argue with her that it is, not only the House of Commons' privilege, but responsibility to deal with money bills. Not in isolation, of course. She will be aware that, while the Senate cannot initiate a money bill, it is part of the parliamentary process that finally achieves its passage. I am sure she was not trying to say that the Senate has no role to play in the passage of money bills. I think I understand the spirit of what she said.
What I do not understand is the minister's contradiction in terms two or three minutes later. With much sound and fury, she said loudly and clearly that she could not respond to the recommendations because of the reasons she had just given. Then she proceeded to respond to some of them. I note the contradiction and the grandstanding that she was not going to be compromised. A few minutes later, she was willing to be compromised on at least a couple of points. So, first, I note the contradiction.
More to the point, and to respond to the hon. member from Carleton-Charlotte who spoke a few moments ago, we commend the minister for the small step she has taken. She heard the Senate in part. Now that she has set the precedent and opened the door, it is possible for a minister in the House to hear some of the things the Senate has said on this issue. Her earlier argument about not being able to respond is obviously swept by the side, because she has responded on at least two details. I appeal to the minister now to review her earlier thinking, go back to look at the Senate message and respond more fully so that we can have a better bill that will serve the people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad that the member finally got back to the motion that is before the House.
I would like to ask him a couple of questions about the Senate. I will not call it the other place, I will call it the Senate because that it what it is.
Government Orders
The Senate has never written a Throne Speech; that is not its function. It has never put together a budget; that is not its function. It has never had to put forward any national program; that is not its function. It has never initiated any economic program. Regardless of this, the Senate is exercising powers beyond its ability to carry them out.
The member has been in the House of Commons for a number of years and knows very well what has happened in the process here. The Senate has proposed amendments that the House of Commons would reject. Had these changes been put forward at committee, they would have been rejected. Had they been put forward at the report stage of the bill, they would have been rejected by the Speaker. Yet, the member and his colleagues are asking the House to accept in the House of Commons amendments that the House would not accept itself by adopting the amendments put forth by the Senate. Does he think it is a proper for the Senate to circumvent the rules of the House this way?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Burlington.
First, in his opening remarks, the hon. member used the phrase "beyond its ability" when talking about the Senate. We should be clear that the Senate has done nothing that is beyond its ability. Let us be fair about that. The framers of the Constitution very clearly provided that the Senate has a role, but that role is limited. It cannot, for example, kill a money bill. It can delay a money bill.
One must ask, if the Senate was given this power, who took it away? Is it the words of the member that takes away the power? Is this some new interpretation of the Senate Act or the House of Commons Act? The question really is this: If the Senate is doing something that is illegal, why is there not a proceeding to challenge that?
I hear the rhetoric and it is great. Perhaps, if I were over there, I would be saying some of the same stuff myself. But it has nothing to do with the reality. The reality is that what the Senate is doing is perfectly within its right. If the Senate is doing something that somebody does not like, that is another issue. But let us not get the two mixed up. It is one thing to have the Senate doing something one finds completely odious from one's point of view, but it is another to characterize it as being beyond its ability or capability under law. That is quite a

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
different issue. Everything the Senate has done here is absolutely proper.
The Senate has a role and was appointed back in 1867 to protect the regions of the country. That is fine as long as everybody is in bed together and the Senate is doing things that everybody likes.
For example, I have not heard anybody say that the Senator Murray has no right to go around the country talking about the Constitution because he was not elected. Senator Murray has had a fairly powerful role there in his capacity as a senator. It is his capacity in the Senate that allows him to be part of the Queen's Privy Council in Canada. In order to be one of the Queen's ministers, he had to be either in the Senate or in the House, and we know he is not in the House. Senator Murray is going around the country in his capacity as a representative of the government. He happens to be a part of that government by virtue of his membership in the Senate.
If there is suddenly this new burst of interest in purifying the system so that unelected people have no role, I will make a deal. Let us bridle Senator Murray and another unelected person, named John Crow. I have never heard anybody around here say that he ought to be elected. He is out there making decisions that are pulverizing my people in terms of their mortgage rates. He is doing that and he has not been elected. But suddenly there is this great urge to have them all elected.
I am watching with great interest how the government is going to do an about-face a few months from now when it cannot get its way as it is trying to do right now. It will suddenly go out and appoint more Senators to do what it says is illegal for the Senate to do in the first place. It cannot have it both ways.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member did not answer my question. I found the same thing with his House Leader. I asked him the same question and he did not answer it. I will ask the hon. member again.
The Senate has put forth amendments to Bill C-21 that would not have been allowed in the House of Commons had they been put at report stage and that would have been struck down had they been put at committee stage. Does he think that legislation that
cannot be amended in this House should be allowed to be amended by the Senate?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I promise the member I will give him a specific yes or no answer in a moment.
First, he threw in some other phrasing that tickles my fancy, as we say back home. He said: "-amendments that cannot be put in this House". I correct him. It is not, that "cannot", but that "were not". They were not passed in this House but there was no lack of capability. This House can amend this document in any way it wants. There is nobody in this Chamber who does not believe that. We can amend it in any way we want because we are the Parliament of Canada. Nobody is going to argue against that. So, first, it can be done here.
My second point is with regard to authorities on the Senate. From the time of its inception, and going back to the first Prime Minister of the country, Mr. MacDonald, when he discussed the role of the Senate, one of the most oft-used characterizations of the Senate is a chamber of sober second thought. It is generally understood that sober second thought is one of the assigned functions of the Senate.
I put to you, Madam Speaker, the following conundrum. If the role of the Senate is to second-think some of the things that this House does-and that presumes that it might suggest changes-how can we give them that role if, in the next mouthful, it says it cannot perform that role. Does it not follow that, if it is the chamber of sober second thought, sometimes it will come back and say: "House of Commons, we have looked at the legislation you have sent to us and we are suggesting the following changes"? Surely, nobody is going to argue that that is not within the role and the prerogative of the Senate. That is what the Senate has done here.
The question that the hon. member for Burlington has put to me, as I understand it, very clearly or at least in sum, was do I think that the Senate has the right to recommend amendments to the House of Commons. The answer is, yes, I think so.
