speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to participate again in debate on Bill C-21. I would hope that members in the House, when listening to other members in debate, would understand the realm
May 8, 1990

and the acceptability of certain comments. I will try to keep mine as parliamentary as I can, unlike some other members of the House in previous debate.
I rise today to debate this bill which is once again back before the House of Commons. It is a bill that has effectively gutted the unemployment insurance program. That is a program that, unfortunately, too many of us in far-flung regions of the country have had to depend on from time to time because of failed economic policies and a lack of government policy and programs to redistribute wealth across the country.
The effect of Bill C-21 is to change the unemployment insurance system forever. What the government has done is to remove itself from participating in the fund. The government has said that from this point on it is going to be an employer-employee fund. The Government of Canada has reneged on its responsibility to look after the unemployed worker in this country. It is a responsibility that has been there since the bill was initially passed by the House of Commons.
What does the bill do? Why are we on this side of the House so opposed to it? The bill does a whole number of things. First, the bill extends the qualifying period in most parts of the country. In effect, what it means is that those poor Canadians from places like Cumberland- Colchester in New Brunswick, parts of eastern Ontario, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Antigonish County who do not have a full-time job, or a regular pay cheque coming in, and who are trying to make ends meet for themselves and their families, now will have to try a little harder. The government says: "We don't think you're trying hard enough to find work. We think that you're living off the system. What we are going to do is punish you. We are going to make you find more weeks of work. Not only that, but if you are able to find work in an area of 15 per cent to 20 per cent unemployment, then we will give you a smaller benefit period. We are going to shorten up the benefit period".
In effect, what the government is doing with this bill is ensuring that those people in this country who have not been able to share the wealth will be the very ones who will be nailed by this government, and not only for retraining, which is quite a departure for this govern-
Government Orders
ment. The government is now saying under this legislation that those who are unemployed should bear the burden of training. Yet it is taking money out of the unemployment insurance fund which is meant as an income support program for those individuals who find hard times in various parts of this country. It is going to increase the qualifying period and decrease the benefit period as well as the benefits. That is what this bill does. It puts the onus strictly on those in our society who are at least able-for the time being-to look after themselves economically.
The bill does a little more than that. When the bill was first introduced in this House last year, in June I believe it was, it was universally condemned by social activists across this country, by provincial premiers and by individuals who work with the poor, the homeless and the downtrodden. The government did not listen.
At one point I asked the minister responsible a question in the House. I indicated that this bill was simply going to force people off UI and on to municipal welfare rolls. The minister in turn got up and indicated that the government was very concerned about helping people on welfare, and that it was allocating more resources to the Canada Assistance Program for welfare recipients.
I do not think that she realized exactly the feeling that she was conveying. The feeling of this government is that if you cannot look after yourself, do not look toward the government to give you that hand. That is a fundamental departure from the way that this country has operated.
This is a wealthy country. We have always believed that we had the resources, the dollars, the heart and the spirit to redistribute our wealth. We have always believed that nobody in this country should go hungry, that if there are hard times they should be borne by all. That was the principle of the UIC act. It was an income support program.
The bill did not come back from the Senate as quickly as the government would have wanted. The Senate was quite clearly doing its job. The Senate is the other part of Parliament. This is the House of Commons. As everybody should know here, bills get introduced, go through the House and then they go to the other place for sober second thought, for thorough debate.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
Anybody who wishes to misinterpret or mislead Canadians into believing that the Senate is only there for rubber stamping, absolutely denies the history of the Parliament of Canada. In many occasions in the past the Senate, when it had a bill, would do what it was constitutionally obliged to do. It was to take it through all stages in the Senate, which includes committee. In many cases when a government has not been responsive to the needs and wishes of Canadians, the Senate, unelected as it is, has tried to do its part for the democratic process.
The democratic process means that when legislation gets introduced in Parliament, by the time it is finished it has gone through all readings in both Chambers, that it has the benefit not just of debate and committee work in this place, but the benefit of committee work in the other place. I challenge anybody in this House to stand up and tell me with a clear conscience, knowing that they would be misleading, that the Senate does no work of any value.
The Senate of Canada has produced some of the most advanced committee work that have helped this place, helped our policy areas and the government in formulating social and economic policies than this place has done.
When the bill went over to the Senate the government could not get its way. This government is hell-bent on pushing everything through. If you do not agree with the government, it tries to shut you down. If you really want to get to the crux of the matter, the government knew that it did not have public opinion on its side on Bill C-21. It knew that what it was doing was wrong. It knew that what it was doing was unpopular. It knew that what it was doing was in effect kicking in the butt those Canadians who are least able to defend themselves.
The government wanted the Senate, unelected as it is, to be like tame dogs who were going to be scared off from doing their job by some of the rhetoric flowing from the front benches opposite. The government wanted the Senate to deal with it expeditiously. Members of the government said: "Don't listen to Canadians because we on this side have stopped listening. We have plugged our ears and we just go forward with legislation. You nasty old Senators who are trying to do your job, unelected as you are, in ensuring that Canadians are heard ensure that legislation goes through both Houses and that the
end result is that the legislation that is passed into law is legislation of the very best kind".
Thus it goes over to the Senate of Canada. The Senate says: "Hey, there is something wrong here. The government is being negligent in its responsibility to this program. The government in effect is dismantling a major piece of social policy legislation in this country. We think we have to study it. If the Tory government has an agenda whereby it is going to tiy to depopulate those regions of Canada where we have some difficulty with employment and, yes, unfortunately, where we have to look for a handout now and then, if that is what the idea is, then the Senate of Canada feels it is in the best interest of those regions that this bill get a full and thorough airing through the committee process and through debate".
I think that the Senate is really there to represent the interests of the regions, to ensure that they are not trampled on by an out of control government which is just concerned about pleasing its big business buddies down on Bay Street, just concerned about serving the centre. I am sure at some point there must have been a debate in the Tory caucus, or at least in planning and priorities, to figure out how in the name of God you can get rid of all these welfare recipients down east and what to do with these northerners who keep looking for more money. The government says: "My goodness, don't they know that this country has to be run like a business?" At least the Senate knows that this country cannot always be run like a business. There are costs to keeping a country together. You must treat a country and run a country like a nation.
If you run a country like a nation, instead of like a Bay Street business all the time, then you ensure that there are social programs in place for those who are most in need.
The Senators saw this coming. They said: "Okay, we do not want to frustrate the will of the elected place, the House of Commons, but what we want to do is try to make these guys snap to their senses. Do they not have any idea what they are doing to the poor and the unemployed?"
Madam Speaker, I represent the riding of Dartmouth in Nova Scotia, and I am very lucky to represent that riding. We have some economic difficulties, but by and large it is a riding which has benefited from being the centre of Atlantic Canada. What annoys me the most about the way this government operates and the way it treats people who are not from the royal south of
May 8, 1990

Ontario with $100,000 a year incomes so they can support this government with donations and ads during election campaigns and things like that, is that I come from a place called Cape Breton-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Silly ass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Silly what? I think there was a comment from the hon. member opposite. If he wants to say it a little louder, we can get it into Hansard.
I come from a place called Cape Breton Island, New Waterford to be exact. It is a coal mining community. We have seen more dinner times than we have seen dinners down there. But we are hard workers. Probably I grew up in poverty. I did not know it because everybody else who lived on the same street, the same neighbourhood and the whole town was poor. At times we had to rely on the generosity and the heart of the federal government to get us through hard times. At times even my father had to go on unemployment insurance. If UI ran out, maybe he had to go on relief from the coal company. But those programs were there to help those communities and those individuals who wanted to contribute.
The whole intent of this legislation is to ensure that we are businesslike. Maybe, just perhaps, it is to ensure that there is a resettlement, that we can get those guys down east-who these people opposite think are perpetually on unemployment insurance and are poor because we want to be poor, which is nonsense and gutterwash-to finally come to their senses, if the government cuts off all the strings of support. I think somebody in this Chamber said a little earlier that they will either move or starve.
We have seen this over and over again by this government. It has no idea where it is going, other than to the centre. It has no other agenda than to cut those bloodsuckers off, those people who are perpetually and habitually draining tax dollars through social programs.
This bill was debated at one point in the fall, and I refer to an article from The Globe and Mail written by Susan Delacourt on October 10. I just want to give members opposite an idea of what they are doing to rural Canada. I want to give them an idea of what they are
Government Orders
doing to areas that have perpetually suffered from high levels of unemployment.
The headline states: "New jobs policy angers Newfoundland. Shift to training viewed as disguised resettlement program". We can all get up here and spout off rhetoric, and we are all equally good on all sides of this House. But there is now a feeling in Atlantic Canada that we are no longer wanted by this government to stay in Atlantic Canada, and that just perhaps we are no longer wanted by this government as part of Canada. We have all too often had to go down the road to Toronto. Years before my parent's people had to go down the road to Boston. Only a few years ago we had to go down the road to Alberta. Now what this government is doing with Bill C-21 is trying to ensure that we go down the road forever.
As the former Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Turner said in a speech he gave a number of months back: "This government seems hell-bent on turning Atlantic Canada into one gigantic national park, devoid of industry, devoid of hope and devoid of people".
The Senate got hold of this bill. It said: "This is a fundamental shift away from Canadian social policy. Maybe we can shake this government awake and tell it what the impact is". Maybe the Senate can tell the government what the impact is in Nova Scotia where the changes to the UI act, which the Minister of Employment so smugly got up to defend in this House, are going to cost Nova Scotians in real dollar terms about $50 million. That is a lot of money in a province of about 870,000 people, coupled with the $80 million cut in the second last budget to EPF funding that goes to hospitals and post-secondary education.
The government says in this bill: "We are doing this because we want to put more emphasis on training". It cannot have it both ways. You cannot tell us that your cutting is not gutting a bill and hurting us economically in places like Atlantic Canada and at the same time say: "We are concerned about training. That is why we have done it". If you are so concerned about education, programs and training, then why in the name of goodness have you cut $80 million from the Established Programs Financing over the next five years in Nova Scotia alone?

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
That is money that goes to training to make sure that we have a well educated, highly skilled workforce.
I am just trying to give you, Madam Speaker, an idea of the full impact of this legislation, coupled with the other regressive measures. We found out two weeks ago that there was $50 million less transferred in equalization program payments to Nova Scotia.
We found out in the last 12 months that there was $1,221 billion in economic regional development agreements in Atlantic Canada that have been allowed to expire. Yet the minister opposite from Nova Scotia, from Central Nova, the minister responsible for those agreements, only put up $274 million. By anybody's calculation that is almost a $1 billion shortfall.
The effect of this bill, if members opposite do not come to their senses and sit down and talk to the Senate about refining the bill further, is not just going to be that a few people will have to move to Toronto. The effect of the bill is real hardship.
I do not know if members opposite who come from wealthier ridings have ever had to deal with somebody whose benefits have run out and who could not get employment. I dealt with a lot of them when I used to work for my colleague from Cape Breton-East Richmond many years ago. He comes from one of the higher unemployment areas in the country. I will tell you that the gentleman from Cape Breton-East Richmond has worked hard on behalf of those constituents to try to bring this government to its senses and to show it the real human tragedy in suffering and deprivation that is going to be caused by this bill.
Has anybody opposite ever had to sit down with a young gentleman of 22 who has two children and is living in a barn in October when the winds howl down off the east coast of Atlantic Canada because there is no work? You tell me that that man enjoys that. You tell me that he enjoys going to bed at night knowing that he cannot look after his spouse and his children. That is the impression I get from listening to speeches by members opposite.
When this bill came into the House I was annoyed. I was damn mad when I listened to some members opposite talk about the abuse of the UI system. Sure, there is abuse. There is abuse in every program, but it is a
very small percentage of abuse. To correct the abuse, as they call it, they have nailed everybody.
If they have ever had to sit down at 4.30 on a Friday afternoon when every municipal and provincial government office that can help is closed and look in the eye a guy with two small boys, four and two, who is living in a barn because the system has failed him, I do not think they could stand in their places opposite and say that those people who are on unemployment insurance do not need it, that if they worked a little harder they would find a job. The reality of today's economy in those areas is otherwise.
This government is completely abandoning the principle of trying to help those individuals who need the help the most.
The amendments that have been proposed by the Senate are truly amendments not meant to frustrate the will of Parliament. They are amendments meant to put some heart and some sense back into the heads and bodies of the members opposite in the government, to try to show them what the full impact of these measures is.
What in the name of goodness are we going to do when people can no longer get the weeks work that they need to go on unemployment insurance, when they cannot get the extra qualifying weeks? How in the name of goodness are those municipalities that are now going to have to pay welfare to them going to find the money?
This government's cut-backs have cut us to the bone in Atlantic Canada. They have pummelled those that need this government's help the most.
I want to talk very quickly about the Senate. The Senate has been trying to do its job. It has been trying to save the hides of the members opposite here who are now down to 15 per cent in public opinion because of their misguided policies. Perhaps if they listened to the Senate, which has every constitutional right to do what it is doing on this particular bill, they would not be at 15 per cent in the polls. Perhaps they could sleep a little bit sounder at night. Perhaps they could come to their senses and withdraw legislation like this and put heart and caring back into government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology

speechtext:
Can the member tell me what the employment situation was in 1984 and what it is now in Atlantic Canada?
May 8, 1990

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1984 were just recovering from a recession. Because of Liberal policies people were not lined up at food banks like they are now in Atlantic Canada.
In 1984, because of Liberal policies, which were a safety net in case of recession so that nobody in this country should go hungry or lose their home, they worked. He asks me now what the situation is. The situation is bleak in places like Cape Breton Island. The situation is absolutely desperate in places like Cumberland-Colchester. The situation is absolutely devastating in our fisheries communities across Atlantic Canada.
I hope the hon. member was just trying to fill time when he asked the question because I am going to fill in a little bit of time for him. He asked what the situation now is dealing with unemployment in Atlantic Canada.
If you want to look at the real tragedy in Atlantic Canada, look at the measure that was put forward yesterday by a whole bevy of ministers. I thought they were delivering the federal treasury, there were so many down there for the announcement. My goodness, we had to wait weeks for the hon. Minister for International Trade to come back to get his value photo opportunity.
Yesterday what we were waiting for was a rescue package, an aid package for the fisheries which has been in a state of virtual collapse in Atlantic Canada. It did not happen yesterday. If the hon. member has been in this House since the election of 1988, he knows that members on this side of the House have been consistently standing in their places and doing everything but begging this government to recognize the crisis that was emerging in the Atlantic fishery.
Do you want to know what the situation is now with a Tory government in power? We have the town of Canso ready to go down on its knees after being shut down after 400 years of fishing tradition. We have Trepassey, Gaul-tois, Lockeport and a whole number of other small communities that have lost their single industry-fisheries. It is a resource-based industry that when managed properly can allow people to eke out a modest living.

This government, which is so uncaring about any industry in Atlantic Canada, did not listen to the members over here. As a result, we are seeing a social tragedy unfold. We are seeing a resettlement program.

Madam Speaker, it is very important to me to have this opportunity to comment on Bill C-21 which is now back before us in the House of Commons. I say that because there is a rumour going about the country that everything is okey-dokey in
May 8, 1990

Toronto, that we do not have poor people in Toronto, that we do not have unemployed or hungry people in Toronto. As I say, that is a rumour. You can see hungry people at the food lines. You will not see many of the unemployed people because they cannot pay the Toronto rents. They are forced out of sight, out of Toronto. The 10,000 to 20,000 homeless people still lurking around Toronto are not telephoned by Statistics Canada to find out whether they have a job or not. They do not have a job. They do not have a telephone. They do not have a home to put a telephone in.
This piece of legislation is quite untimely. No doubt it is a good thing to create jobs but not to take money from people who have paid their unemployment insurance premiums on the excuse of training them for new jobs.
We know what the neo-Conservative agenda is, and we know with unemployment insurance the primary goal is to weaken the bargaining power of workers, to cause more workers to lose their rights to unemployment benefits, to cause workers to be uneasy about standing up for their rights on the job because the rules have changed for dismissing a person and for taking away a person's benefits after he or she has been dismissed.
What this government is looking for and obviously what it has promised the Business Council on National Issues is a more docile work force where people will not stand up and defend themselves as vigorously as they have done over the past decades. By taking the money from the pockets of the unemployed to do the training the government is depriving the unemployed. Many unemployed will not get the training and there is no guarantee given by the government that they will. In the short term the government is depriving the unemployed of the benefit from premiums they paid. It is also putting those who do take training in the position of having taken it from their brothers and sisters by the government's order. This will mean a meaner and less generous program.
The current President of the United States said he wanted a gentler, kinder country. He obviously thinks that is Canada. That is why he is taking it over, but we
Government Orders
will not be a gentler, kinder country once we have been homogenized into the American pattern.
The primary fault of this system is the removal of the government from any responsibility, the responsibility it has had for nearly half a century, for not only administering the fund but also for providing input as a guarantee of both regional fairness and carryover in times of slump. The government until now has had a material interest in seeing that unemployment does not become serious.
Now the government, if this bill is passed, will go scot-free and will be able to let unemployment rise without a bill to the government for payment.
This Tory government has shown its intention by holding the present unemployed hostage to the VERs. Instead of the annual adjustment of benefits and the eligibility time to the current regional conditions, the government has tied these benefits to the bill in which it will take this $1.3 billion out of the fund created primarily by workers and employers.
The government will not review the VERs. It is now May and it still refuses to review the VERs. It will not review parental benefits in spite of a Supreme Court decision ordering it to provide them. It is showing itself in contempt of the law of the land, which it brags about. The government says we have a government according to law, only according to the laws which suit the government. As I say, they are holding the training funds hostage. There are no training funds yet because the government has cut back on most of the training programs that we have had during the 1980s. They are holding hostage the entire principle of training.
Yesterday the minister spoke at length about the importance of training. Nobody disagrees that training is important. Nobody disagrees that for our economy to sustain itself there must be training and retraining. What she did not mention yesterday was that the six labour-business task forces that she set up to make recommendations about the new training program all said: "Don't take unemployment insurance money to do it".
She brags about having set up these task forces. She brags about the training programs, but she ignored the unanimous recommendation of her own task forces on that point.

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
As I have said, there is a rumour about the country that everything is just lovely in Toronto. In fact in the last couple of years Toronto has lost about 77 plants, either closed or on notice of closing. This puts about 16,000 workers in jeopardy, either out of work or about to be out of work. Simply talking about the number of jobs does not answer the question of how these people can pay the cost of living in Toronto, how they can pay Toronto rents or house prices. A job at McDonald's doesn't do that in Toronto.
It is going to be the older workers particularly in Toronto who will be hit. Many of these plants have a great many long service employees or had until they were closed a great many long service employees. I know from my own experience. When the factory I worked in was closed down after about a half-century of operation, men and women 50 years or older had a very hard time finding other work, particularly if they had a few little injuries on the job. A tow motor operator with a bad back is not much sought after by the employers, especially if he is looking for something other than tow motor work because there are not that many tow motor jobs.
finding whatever benefits are due to them as well as opportunities for training and retraining, training in English or French as a second language and retraining in their own industry such as the clothing industry or for other industries that are emerging or increasing and in which these people might find jobs.
The Metro Toronto Labour Education Centre has found that among the workers who come to it for help the average length of unemployment after a plant closing is 10 months. Out of all the new jobs we are told about the average is 10 months to find a new job after a lay-off. The reduced benefits in Bill C-21 will mean that the maximum a worker can get will be 35 weeks or just over 8 months and that is in Toronto. Madam Speaker, 6 weeks of holidays without pay is not what these workers are looking for. When you live on unemployment insurance you are not saving very much money. Many of these workers are going to be over the 10-month mark, and they and their families will suffer a good deal. How do they pay a mortgage with nothing coming in?
Immigrants and people with very little formal education will be hard hit. The policies of the present and past governments of allowing the people to drift out of the homes they want to live in on the east coast into places like Toronto have brought many people with limited schooling; not all of them but many of them. I worked with them in the factory for 18 years. Their schooling was limited; good as far as it went, but it does not take them beyond grade 7 or grade 8 in most cases. Many immigrants and people with little education will be very hard hit. They will not find it easy to get jobs to pay their mortgages. Of course, once they have had to move out of Toronto, the government will again say that the Toronto statistics look good.
There is a great deal of good work being done by the Metro Toronto Labour Education Centre. On this point I do want to commend the minister for her continued funding of that work. They are doing the kind of work that the minister and the government and members on this side of the House agree should be done. They get in touch with workers. They encourage workers to get in touch with them when they have been laid off or are about to be laid off. They can give them assistance in
As I said, in Toronto the housing prices and mortgage prices are seriously overheated. We also have in Toronto a significant number of the visible minority population. This government has expressed its concern, and rightly so. Other people are expressing concern about rising racial tensions in our country. We have the evidence of that in Toronto, as elsewhere. This is going to be exacerbated by the government's action in this bill. The increased penalties for those who quit their jobs could be really devastating for people who suffer from subtle racism.
In other words, if a person of a visible minority or for that matter a woman, let alone a woman of a visible minority, is being harassed on the job because of race or gender-and it happens; I have seen it in the factory and I am sure many others in this House have seen it in different places of work-it is going to be very hard to know whether he or she should stand up for themselves and risk losing the job under these new harsher penalties or whether they should button their lips and accept the racist or sexist harassment just so that they know that they will have a pay cheque next week and the week after.

May 8, 1990

This bill will make their situations harder. It will make it harder for them to stand up against the kind of racial discrimination or gender discrimination that all sides of this Parliament are opposed to.
This bill will also have the effect of forcing workers into substandard jobs, if they can get them at all. The Labour Education Centre has reported that those who re-entered the workforce in Toronto after a plant closure got a job that averaged $3 per hour less than the one they left. They were the lucky ones who got another job, but they now have to make do and pay that mortgage with $3 an hour less. Just to say there are jobs there does not tell people whether or not they can live or whether or not they can keep a roof over their heads in the city of Toronto.
It is possible that the government does not pay much attention to the findings of the Labour Education Centre or to the Downtown Churchworkers' Association which were refused the right to speak to the committee last year when they came to Toronto. But the government usually professes to pay some attention to the Economic Council of Canada. In its recent report Good Jobs: Bad Jobs the council reports that for Canada as a whole 54 per cent of those who changed jobs after the age of 55 were still unemployed six months later. More than half the older workers 55 years of age or older who changed jobs were still unemployed six months later. That is, if they had to leave a job it was six months or more before they found another. At that age, that is very threatening. Some of us here know what it is like to be in our late fifties and sixties or even seventies.
It also reported that 40 per cent of the workers of all ages who were laid of suffered a wage loss. We are talking in many cases about workers with years of service, experienced workers, laid off through no fault of their own but through changing business conditions. Two out of five of them suffered a wage loss. Many of these people are living just on the edge of making it on Toronto rents, transporation prices, and general Toronto costs. The Economic Council of Canada also reports that the gap in the unemployment rate between those with less than nine years of schooling and the average has widened significantly over the past decade.
Fortunately, schooling is increasing and the average is now more than nine years. That is good, but the wage gap for those who did not make it past nine years of schooling is increasing and they have to suffer under the
Government Orders
same living costs in Toronto as those with higher education who are getting the jobs with the rising incomes that are increasing the gap between them and the rest.
My point is that it will be the older workers, the less educated workers, and the workers who have been laid off following the many plant closures related to free trade who will be suffering more as a result of Bill C-21. A few of them may get into the training programs we have been told about. As I said, the minister does not guarantee that any of them will. Certainly the minister does not try to tell us that all or most of them will have that opportunity.
The effect of this bill is to take money from those who generally can least afford it, in order to train people to serve those who in many cases are paying no or almost no taxes. This government has a powerful track record over the last five or six years of reducing the tax on those who have the most ability to pay and increasing the tax on those who have the least ability to pay.
This bill is another tax on those who have the least ability to pay. Yes, some of them may be trained, but the people who will employ them will in many cases be those whom this government is excusing from paying the cost of that training. Instead it is forcing their relatively poorer brothers and sisters who continue in the work force or who were in the work force paying unemployment insurance benefits to pay that cost. It will force the poor to subsidize the poorer, while the rich will pay less and less, especially if the goods and services tax is imposed.
These 80,000 or 90,000 companies that pay no tax will be able to employ workers who are trained at the cost of others. They will not have to pay the cost of training. It is a very unjust law set within a pattern of unjust laws. There are high taxes on working people. There are high interest rates that put mortgages beyond the reach of many working people. Now we have an unemployment insurance system that will take from the poor to subsidize the training of a few workers to the benefit of the rich. It is a shameful law.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I will not go into it in great detail but I will point out for example that in Trinity-Spadina many thousands of the people are immigrants from Hong Kong, the People's Republic of China, or the several countries of southeast Asia. These are mostly people who come with little knowledge of English or French. Their employment is often limited by their opportunities within the community of their own languages.
In past years it has certainly been found that some of these people were working at below minimum wage and were being deprived of benefits such as unemployment insurance by unscrupulous employers. Many of them are working in the garment industry which has suffered greatly from this government's action in the trade deal with the United States. If they find their place of employment closed they will have a harder than average time finding work somewhere else because in many cases, particularly among the women, they have not had an opportunity to learn English.
The policy of this government and of the previous government was to provide some English language training for those who were destined for the workforce. That means they excluded people whom they regarded as mere housewives. They could just stay home. They did not need English. That is by and large the policy, especially as the government is cutting back on English and French as second language programs.
People such as that have been held back by their working conditions because not all those housewives had the luxury of staying home every day, if that is what they considered a luxury. Many of them, nevertheless, had to
get out to work to pay the rent and to make ends meet. They did not have the opportunity to learn one of the official languages, to learn what is the minimum wage amount, to learn other basic laws of our country for the protection of workers so that they could defend themselves and their rights on the job. Those people will suffer considerably.
There are other language minorities as well. There are people who speak a dialect of the Caribbean; there are people from the Azores and from the mainland of Portugal; there are others from various non-Englishspeaking countries, all of whom to some degree suffer the same difficulty as these East Asian immigrants. They will bear an extra cost under this Bill C-21 if it becomes law.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. I just want to repeat some elementary points, not respecting the substance of Bill C-21 which has been debated for many months in this House and in committee and in the other place, but rather the propriety of the actions of the Senate respecting this legislation.
We have had the benefit of the Chair's ruling that was requested by myself in respect of the actions of the Senate. As the Speaker very clearly pointed out in his ruling, that while he lacked, as we understood, the constitutional authority to intervene with the other House, just as the Speaker of the other House lacks the authority to intervene here, there was no question that what the Senate is proposing tramples substantially on the rights and privileges of this House.
First, the financial initiative of the Crown is infringed when, in the Senate's proposed changes in Bill C-21, major costly amendments are proposed without first securing a Royal Recommendation. It seems clear to any fair-minded person who looks at the legislation that the Royal Recommendation is exceeded vastly by the proposed amendments of the Senate.
Second, there is an affront by the Senate to this House when Senators in the majority ignore and defy the budget and its valence of Ways and Means. They have suggested in Bill C-21 that they can make changes to the unemployment insurance system which take an additional $1.75 billion out of the revenue this year and upset the budget proposed by this House to that extent. This is not
Government Orders
just a minor adjustment, this is a $2 billion hole in the budget projections from April 1989, a budget from last year.
Third, as a result of the two basic constitutional shortfalls I have cited, the Senate puts itself in violation of the principles in Sections 53 and 54 of our Constitution Act. It might be helpful just to remind this House what those sections say because this is our constitution. They state that bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue or for imposing any tax impost shall originate in the House of Commons.
That right becomes meaningless if the other place can distort and change to an extent as to make the origin unrecognizable. What good is it to have this authority in the constitution if the other place assumes to itself the authority to distort and warp what might have been initiated in this House.
Section 54 states that it shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or at any tax impost to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message of the Governor General, the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed. That is the so-called Royal Recommendation.
If it is unlawful for this House to depart from the Royal Recommendation, how can one suggest that the other place can do so? How can we possibly accept amendments from the other House which we cannot accept if they were proposed in this House. What constitutional authority would make it appropriate for us to accept amendments from the other place which we could not accept if they originated in this place? That surely is not a procedure that anyone who respects this institution could voluntarily agree to.
Finally, for these reasons, the motion of the government makes it very clear that this House will not turn its back on the law and the constitution and our own long-established procedures here. We say in the message that we will not accept Senate proposals which cost money over which only this elected House has the power to propose.
The other place claims its authority from Section 17 of the British North America Act, or the Constitution of Canada Act, which says, "There shall be a Parliament

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
consisting of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons."
The Chair affirmed in the ruling of April 26, 1990, that the strength of our parliamentary system lies in all three constituent parts respecting their constitutional roles. Section 17 could be interpreted by the Governor General to mean that he has the right to amend legislation, to alter it, to change it, to kill it, or veto it, and those who support the Senate's right to do that, must also support the Governor General's right to do that.
What kind of a democratic system would that be? Obviously an absurd democratic system that has never, ever in this country, until 1984, been a part of the practice.
I would like to refer the House to a paragraph from a book, The Modern Senate of Canada, published in 1965. That is the latest reference we have to the modern Senate. This is pre-MacEachen, obviously. It is by Mr. EA. Kunz. After a long discussion about the relative roles of the House and the Senate, he states:
On the contrary, the Senate has acted in full understanding of 1he meaning and implications of responsible government and accepted as binding upon itself the proposition that it should not unduly disturb what has come to be called "the balance of ways and means"; or, as Hopkins says, "that it would be inadmissible to tamper with the overall financial program submitted by the Government in its budgetary proposals in such a way as to effect a material change in the budgetary surplus or deficit envisaged therein".
Surely the Senate's proposal of a $2 billion increase in the deficit is, by anybody's definition, tampering with the balance of ways and means. We have a budget presented in this House. Immediately upon presenting the budget, a motion of confidence is put to the House. It is debated for six days, and there are usually a couple of amendments from the opposition. This House says in finality that, yes, this House has confidence in the budgetary measures of the government.
On the strength of that motion, taxes are collected immediately. Plans are made by industry, by the private sector, by the economy of this country. This is possible because of all these practices, such as provisions 53 and 54 of the Constitution. It has been the practice for more than a century in this country and a few centuries in Britain, upon which our system is based, that the
unelected chamber does not tamper with the balance of ways and means. Until 1984, that was the way this country operated.
In 1984, some Trudeauites were appointed to the Senate and now, suddenly, we are having a debate which is more fitting for Victorian England than modem Canada. It is incredible in this day and age, in 1990, that we are seriously discussing whether in fact an elected legislature should have precedence over a non-elected body. It is incredible to find an outstanding lawyer from Kingston, such as the member for Kingston and the Islands, stand there, without blushing, and suggest that it is legitimate for this non-elected, appointed body to trample on the rights of this House.
I would like to acquaint members of the House with Standing Order 80(1), which states:
80. (1) All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought 1o begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
Were we to take the suggestions of the Liberals or the New Democratic Party to accept the Senate's amendments or ask them to go further, we would in essence be going against the Standing Orders of this House.
That Standing Order, by the way, has been there since 1867. It is based on a statement by the British House of Commons in 1671. We have over 300 years of tradition here that says this House and only this House has the right to decide the details on all grants and aids to her Sovereign. The language there is a bit archaic, the argument is a bit archaic, but it is astounding that we should, in all seriousness, be having this debate here.
I suspect that a lot of this is primarily fluff from those people who say that they believe that the Senate is doing good work, that the Senate knows what the people want, the House of Commons does not. But if you read what they say in private or to the media, you get some interesting quotes. Let me quote a few: Senator MacEa-chen, Question Period, 1985, speaking in respect to a borrowing bill that the Senate was then holding up stated: "I think if we did amend the bill in any serious
May 8, 1990

way, or if we defeated it, I think that would be quite arrogant".
Senator MacEachen is the leader of the Liberals in the Senate. Senator Frith is his deputy leader, and he stated: "There may be 100 reasons why we should not in the Senate yield to the House, and only one reason why we should, and if that one reason is that the Commons is elected and the Senate is not, that is reason enough to yield." He is right.
Senator Hebert, remember him?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Senator Buckwold, who is chairing the committee on the GST stated: "It should be understood constitutionally that basically the House of Commons in the end would be supreme, that there could be a very real cause for concern if the Senate rejected bills".
Senator Theriault, a Liberal from New Brunswick, stated: "The House of Commons is the legislature with the powers, as it should be as long as the Senate is an appointed Senate". He is dead right.
Senator DeBane, stated: "The Liberal party was not elected to government. The Conservatives were. It is time to bow to the will of the elected representatives. I urge my colleagues not to put any more road-blocks in the way of passing this bill".
New Democratic Party House leader, Nelson Riis, said on October 30, 1987: "Quite frankly, I am very disappointed with the Senate because I do not think it has the right to hold up legislation".
Lome Nystrom, New Democratic Party finance critic in The Globe and Mail, March 28, 1990, said: "I believe the Commons should have the final say. I do not think the unelected body should usurp the elected body".
Pierre Trudeau, remember him, in 1984, when speaking on behalf of that party said: "No member of this Chamber would suggest that the Senate should systematically obstruct the will of the majority in the elected body of Parliament". Pierre Trudeau said that.
Government Orders
Perhaps it is time to acknowledge that there are a lot of things said in this Chamber about this and that, but the reality is that we all serve the public here in this Chamber, or even down the hall, and we serve that public not at all unless we continue to recognize that in a democracy it is only the elected body that has the right to insist that its views prevail.
I do not expect the members of the opposite side to stand up and acknowledge that fact at this point in time.
I expect they will continue to vote that we listen to the Senate and that the Senate has a right to prevail. I understand that. But they do that in the sure knowledge that they are outnumbered in this Chamber. However, I would ask of them that as they meet in caucus with their Senators that they remember that this is a democracy. We are at the end of the day. It is time to let the will of the democratically elected House of Commons prevail. To do otherwise is to do damage to at least 130 years of tradition in this country and a couple of centuries more in terms of the British system upon which our system is based.
I ask that hon. members opposite aid us in ensuring that democracy continues.
