speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was rather interesting listening to the diatribe of the government House leader, particularly in response to the questions which were put to him by my colleague for Kingston and the Islands.
However, in reviewing the motion before the House, I would like indicate to members present that the subject matter that we are dealing with, although very important to Canadians generally, specifically it is very important to those Canadians who have had opportunities, and some of them unfortunate opportunities, to be on unemployment insurance.
Many of those individuals are quite cynical about this entire process, especially the government's actions with regard to the statements that it has made previously. I remind members opposite and the public at large what a senior minister of the Crown said during the last election. The Minister for International Trade said during the 1988 election campaign: "No one is planning any changes in the unemployment insurance program. There has not been any change proposed to us since we dealt with the Forget commission. We are not contemplating any changes".
Those were the words of the Newfoundland representative in the federal cabinet, stating that there would be no changes to unemployment insurance. This was quoted in the Evening Telegram of October 14, 1988, on page 3.
Here we are, not too many months later, with the government introducing a budget and a particular bill to deal with the Unemployment Insurance Commission which will have, in the estimation both of government members, as expressed in this Chamber, and by those who have been recipients of unemployment insurance, tremendous, economic impact on the economies of the various provinces across this country.
As a result of this particular bill, the Government of Canada and the Department of Employment and Immigration have said that the province of Newfoundland will lose $21 million. The Canadian Labour Congress, on the other hand, states that it will be much more significant than $21 million. They state that it will be $58 million. In Nova Scotia it will be $29 million. The Canadian Labour

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
Congress states that it will be $52 million. In Prince Edward Island, CLC states that it will be $22 million; New Brunswick, $47 million; Quebec, $256 million; Ontario, $228 million; Manitoba, $42 million; Saskatchewan, $23 million; Alberta, $60 million; British Columbia, $72 million, for a total of some $800 million, which is a very significant amount.
When I think of young people, such as a young gentleman by the name of Christopher Chisholm who is watching tonight, I wonder what his world will be like 15 to 18 to 20 years from now. What the government has done by presenting this bill is change unilaterally the social contract that Canadians, both employers and employees had with the Government of Canada since the inception of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
The changes which were put forward in the bill received vigorous debate in the House of Commons, examination by legislative committee, and were brought back to the House and thereafter debated in detail. The bill passed in the House because the government has the majority. It went on to the Senate, where the Senate did a thorough analysis, and heard from a variety of groups, including provincial governments, interested spokespersons, and organizations from across the country. They submitted what they believed were honest criticisms, and no one has doubted or questioned their sincerity, or that the facts that they did provide were authentic.
The Senate has made recommendations to this House. In part, the government has accepted some and has not accepted others. We find ourselves in a dilemma with the motion that is before us now to send certain information back to the Senate. The Government of Canada believes that somehow the Senate of Canada does not have the right to do what it is doing. That is understandable. Any time that an institution and individuals in that institution impede progress-and there is a funny way to define progress in this particular instance-that governments want to have in order to change massively the social contract that was so much a part of daily Canadian lives, it is understandable that the big corporate interests and the Conservative Party of Canada would not be pleased
at all with those particular musings and suggestions coming from the other place.
As I said previously in this Chamber on this particular subject matter, these arguments have been made repeatedly by members in this House, by organizations and, of course, by the other place.
The government has a very easy way out of this particular mess they it has got itself into. Page 241 of Beauchesne's fifth edition states:
When the House of Commons does not agree to the Senate amendments, it adopts a motion which states reasons for its disagreement.
Well, that has been done.
This is communicated to the Senate. If the Senators persist in their amendments, they send a message informing the House of this fact. Upon this, the House either accepts the amendments or adopts a motion requesting a conference to which each House appoints Members; and a date is fixed for their meeting.
If members opposite want a way out of this particular impasse of their own making, it is very clear. Either accept the amendments of the Senate or you have a conference. It is a simple as that.
I point out to members opposite and to the public at large that this government does not know how to govern. They do not want to meet. They do not want to discuss. The Senate has eveiy legal and constitutional right to do this, although they can argue the opposite. Quite frankly, we can argue on our side as well, but it is very clear from Beauchesne's fifth edition on page 241 that the appropriate procedure is for a conference to take place and/or for the House of Commons to accept the amendments of the Senate.
Let us not be fooled. We are not just dealing with some sort of procedural wrangling taking place between two separate bodies of one institution, namely the Parliament of Canada. We are dealing with something which is far more important than a procedural wrangling. We are dealing with the lives of Canadians across this country.
I do not say that I and I alone, because I represent a constituency in this country which has excessively high unemployment, know everything about unemployment insurance or that I have the measure of sensitivity and concern of every working man and woman in this country, but I do know that these changes being pro-
May 8, 1990

posed by the government are unacceptable to those individuals who are presently unemployed, who may have been unemployed, and who are likely to be unemployed, because they know the importance which is associated with removing the Government of Canada from the previous tripartite social contract that we had in this country for many years.
To say to employees who work in a fish plant that they as employees will have to pay for the training for high tech workers in downtown Toronto or in Edmonton or in Montreal or Toronto, for the Government of Canada to exclude itself, as a result of the amendments which the government is seeking through this bill, is unfair. We, on this side of the House, believe that it is poor public policy.
Members can debate whether that is accurate, whether it is true or whether it is untrue, but the fact of the matter is that when you remove a major economic player such as the Government of Canada from a tripartite agreement-I call it the social contract-it is no wonder that we have such consternation, such difficulties here in the House and the upper chamber with regard to these particular amendments before us.
The changes which are being sought, not only by members on this side of the House but indeed by the majority of those in the upper House are reasonable, are desired by those who are unemployed and those who work with the unemployed. These changes are being sought by provincial governments and by individuals of different walks of life who know of the insecurities and concerns that unemployed people have in terms of conducting their daily lives.
I would have hoped that the government opposite would have seen its way, notwithstanding its argument which, in some ways, is valid. The budget was introduced on April 27, 1989. Thereafter a piece of legislation to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced in the House and then we had the legislative committee, et cetera, and the debate has been taking place. Sadly, I represent a constituency where the real unemployment rate is, in some communities, three, four and five times that of the national average.
Government Orders
Surely to God we as members of Parliament must plug ourselves in and ask whether this is good public policy.
Members opposite, because of their neo-conservative views, may say that it is, but the majority of Canadians say that it is not. Of course, members opposite will ask what our test is for coming to that conclusion. It is very evident. As you travel across the country and meet with the people whom the public policy will eventually affect, they will tell you en masse that the changes sought by the Conservative government of the Prime Minister of the day are not acceptable to them and that the amendments being put forward by the Liberal party here in this Chamber, augmented if you will by those in the other Chamber, are acceptable to the massive number of Canadians.
Provincial governments concur with what we are doing. It is not good public policy. Surely a government, whether it has a majority of five, ten, twenty or thirty individuals, would not want to implement it notwithstanding the devastation that will take place simply because it believes it may have the upper hand in some sort of procedural argument.
In my concluding remarks I might say that I hope the Chamber has gone beyond that. There is no federal election due for two, three years. Surely it is the job of every member of Parliament to express their particular views, right wing, left wing, centre, neo-conservative, what have you. But you have to ask the fundamental question: Is it good public policy? Is it good public policy to have a tripartite social contract, thereafter to change that and to remove the biggest economic player in that tripartite contract? Is that fair to our fishermen on the Atlantic coast?
There is a very subtle view which is expressed, sometimes not in a public way, but in the most sophisticated way that is rather undignified, particularly for those who are unemployed, both men and women. But nowhere is that statement more apropos than in the fishing sector of our Canadian economy.
People in the fishing industry for many, many years have been able to fish on a seasonal basis, particularly in Atlantic Canada. I do not know if they fish in downtown Toronto, I suspect not, but that is due to the geography of the country. On a commercial basis for a livelihood there is not too much fishing on Yonge Street or in

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
Kingston and the Islands, but there is a hell of a lot of fishing on the Atlantic coast. Those fishermen today know what it is like to be out in a small boat without any form of assistance.
What do I mean by that? We have an economic package which the Government of Canada has announced with great fanfare which has been found by most individuals in our region to be totally unacceptable. You make the problem even more difficult for those fishermen by saying: "And by the way, we have now changed the unemployment insurance. We are going to remove the federal government from the tripartite social contract that was there since its inception. We are going to train you in Canso, Nova Scotia, we are going to train you in Trepassey, Newfoundland. We are going to do all wonderful things for you".
They are all going to become barbers. Imagine, barbers. That is what they are going to train them for. Or maybe they are going to train them to become cooks.
It is just not acceptable that a poor fisherman who may work for a short period of time is now going to have to pay money to train, but train for what in these areas? Not only that, the Government of Canada is not even going to be there to assist and to facilitate in the training process. But this is the hook. The government says that it is going to give money for training of individuals all across Canada. It is going to help the people down there. That is how the government phrases it. It is going to help the people down there.
I charge that the public policy of the fisheries package announced by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, aided and abetted by Bill C-21 and members opposite, is nothing more than a smoke and mirrors game for what has become known in this country as and has proven to be the most disruptive public policy one could imagine, namely resettlement: resettlement of people from Atlantic Canada to other parts of Canada, which is totally unacceptable to the Canadian people regardless of where they live. It infringes upon the pith and substance of the constitutional accord of 1981-82. I believe it is a total abrogation of everything the Prime Minister has said as well as members opposite.
I conclude by urging the government to see the error of its ways. It has an opportunity here to resolve a procedural impasse by doing what Beauchesne says in the fifth edition on page 241, that is, either pass the amendments being advocated by the upper chamber and/or sit down and have a conference in order to resolve this particular matter.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise again to speak on this bill. Notwithstanding any comments the minister may have made, I have very carefully reread the motion before the House. It very clearly refers to amendments to Bill C-21, to the principles of the bill and to the objectives of the policy. It goes on to speak at great length about specific sections of the bill. I have absolutely no hesitation in talking about the bill because that is exactly the subject of the motion before us.
I was astonished to hear the minister stand in the House to speak as he did about democracy. I suspect that never in such a short period in Canadian history, since November 1988 when this government took office, has there been such a consistent attack on democracy. It has occurred not in the other place but in this House.
The figures show that at no time since Confederation has closure been used as much as it has since November 1988.1 fail to remember one bill coming into this House that the opposition wished to debate on which the government has not introduced closure and stifled debate, thereby stifling accountability of this government to the people of Canada.
I cannot of one major bill that has passed this House on which there has been any input from the public. On many of them the government has chosen to ignore totally the views of Canadians. It has ignored them on VIA Rail. It has ignored them on the clawback of old age pensions and family allowances. It has ignored them on unemployment insurance, and it has ignored them on the goods and services tax. In fact it has ignored virtually every commitment it made to the Canadian people to get itself elected to this House.
It should not be one bit surprising if the House of sober second thought insists on giving sober second thought to the fact that this government is proceeding in ways that are totally contrary to commitments and to the
May 8, 1990

sacred trust it swore to Canadians that it would be defending and not abandoning.
If anybody needs to be concerned about the commitment to democracy, it is not the other House and it is not the opposition. It is the Government of Canada.
I want to talk a little about justice. The government pretends that this is a bill that is going to improve things for Canadians somehow, and especially for those who most need a little help.
I want to talk about a very fundamental democratic principle, and that is a fact that we have a Constitution in this country and that Constitution contains the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That charter of rights says that people are to be treated equitably. Also the charter says-and this has been in the courts and is in this bill-that the rights to parental leave in this bill is not this government's gift to women, although the women and the unemployed of Canada will be paying for it. It is something the charter requires. This government is playing a game with those rights in this bill as it is doing with a number of other policy issues by withholding from women who are pregnant right now the rights that the courts said they are entitled to have.
The government is using those rights as bargaining chips against which it is introducing other unpopular, damaging, hurtful measures. If the government is committed to the Constitution, committed to human rights in this country, and at all observant of the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada on those rights, it should be pulling that parental leave requirement out of the bill and introducing it today as a separate bill. We on this side of the House can guarantee that those improved parental rights as ordered by the courts would be through this House in 30 seconds. The government does not want to do that, because then what does it have to put as icing on this very unpleasant piece of mud pie so that the people will think there is something good about it?
The government should also ensure that those parental rights are retroactive. It is going to say that it cannot do that because this bill is being held up. It will say that it cannot give pregnant women who may be on maternity leave the same rights as other women who may go on maternity leave the day after the bill is passed. The government will say it cannot give those two groups of
Government Orders
women the same rights because the bill is being held up; it is not passed yet.
That did not stop the government from starting to charge people higher unemployment insurance rates to pay for those parental benefits, to pay for those maternity benefits, and to pay for training that nobody is getting. Those people have been charged that extra money from January 1, even though the programs that money is supposedly going to pay for are not in place. But the government refuses to give rights and benefits to people retroactive to that same January 1.
Similarly the government is using and victimizing the unemployed because it is not getting its way on this bill as fast as it would like. It is requiring that people work longer. It is taking away the variable entrance requirements that make it easier for people in high unemployment regions to qualify for unemployment insurance. It has refused to do what is fair and just to those persons by simply extending the existing variable entrance requirements. Instead, like a little child it is having a temper tantrum and saying: "if we cannot have our way, everybody else is going to suffer too. The unemployed are going to suffer, pregnant women are going to suffer, and we don't care because we don't care about justice".
As has been said over and over again, this bill hurts those who are poorest, hurts those who are least educated and hurts those who have the hardest time in the labour market. It hurts the poorest regions of this country to the point where whole communities will be dying out because of the provisions of this bill.
I live in a region of relative prosperity with a relatively low unemployment rate. That is why it was a privilege for me to travel across this country and to listen and try to respond with sensitivity to the concerns I heard from people who live in fishing communities, from migrant farmers, from the disabled trying to compete in the labour force, and from women trying to get back into the labour force after being out of it for many years and trying to juggle child care responsibilities. We listened, and some of us heard and some of us did not, to the fact that those who can least afford to be hurt any more are going to be hurt by this bill. That is unjust.
Even members on the other side of the House have to admit that a legitimate role of the Senate, one which it is seeking to strengthen, is to represent the views, opinions and interests of the various regions in this country in a

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
more equitable way, perhaps, than they are represented in this House. The Senate is doing that.
It is listening to people from those various regions on how their section of Canada is going to be hurt, and how this bill will harm our concept of a just and compassionate society that provides equal opportunities from coast to coast, no matter how small or large one's community, or how poor or rich one's household.
This bill hurts those who can least afford to be hurt further. Yet, the government refused to include in this bill any provisions that would ensure that those at the lowest end of the pay scale, with the least resources to compete in a changing labour force, would benefit from the training programs which their meagre incomes are going to be drained further to pay for. This government refused to include what it imposes on every federally regulated industry, which is equitable access for women, disabled persons, visible minorities and native Canadians to these training programs.
After refusing that kind of change to the bill, any government that pretends that it is interested in equity or justice or fairness has very few listeners left. This bill that is floating back and forth between the House and the other place makes no requirement whatsoever for any equity in the delivery of those programs, or assurance that they go to those who need them most. Yet it is those people who are paying the cost.
I said that this is a relatively prosperous region with a relatively low unemployment rate. Yet that very prosperity often hides the plight of the poor in prosperous urban centres. I can tell members of the government that being unemployed in an area like the National Capital Region or in a city like Toronto or in any of the better-off communities of our country is no less painful than it is in Canso, or any of the small communities of our country where people are being hurt badly by the government's economic policies. The changes to the unemployment insurance program will make it worse.
In fact, it is often more difficult to be unemployed in a prosperous area because of the higher prices for food, housing and clothing. They do not have the community support structures which we saw across this country to support and help one's neighbours in times of unemployment and hardship in communities where that is a more common problem.
I want to close with just a few comments about the government's lack of frankness with Canadians about this bill. I do not think the government understands training programs. If it did it would not have stripped money out of the Challenge 90 program and diverted it into a program to try to keep kids in high school. Surely the government must understand that for many families and for many children, the difference between whether or not they go back to high school in September is whether they have a summer job.
I know many families where the pressures of family poverty drive young people out into the workforce before they are ready. The summer job that thousands of young people across our country are being denied is often what gives them a stake in their community, a feeling of having a better future, and what sends them back to school in September. Thousands of young people will no longer have that opportunity.
The bill we are debating today, which is the subject of the motion before us, has one purpose, like so many of the actions of this government. It is not to improve training, it is not to improve employment opportunities, it is not to improve parental benefits, it is to grab more money wherever it can and particularly from victims who are vulnerable and least able to resist.
We need only look at the last few months in this House. Where is the money coming from? It is coming from women; women's programs, women's centres. It is coming from people of a different cultural background. Look at the stripping of the heritage language programs, the stripping of the communications mechanisms of native Canadians. It is coming from seniors through the clawback and changes to RRSPs. It is coming from students in a new fee charged on their student loans, loans for which they only qualify because they are too poor to pay their own way through university. It is coming from children through the clawback of the family allowance, and now it is coming from the unemployed.
If I sound indignant, Madam Speaker, it is because I am, on behalf of all those people from whom we heard right across the country. Two members of the government who were with me at those hearings are in the House today. On behalf of all those people from whom we heard, or at least from whom I heard but from whom apparently the government did not hear, I am indignant and I am angry because I think something fundamental about our sense of sharing and caring for each other in
May 8, 1990

this country, not only from rich to poor but from one region to another, is being abandoned. The government is abandoning its responsibility to contribute on behalf of all Canadians and compensate for the negative effects on some people in some parts of the country for its economic policies. I think that is a shame, and I am ashamed that this is happening in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was not going to participate in this debate but after sitting here yesterday listening to the hon. member for Kamloops I put a question to him. In answer to the question he challenged me to stand up and give a speech to explain to him and to the members of his party the duties and obligations of senators and the privileges of the Senate in relation to Commons bills. I said that of course if the hon. member for Kamloops wanted some advice in that regard I would be happy to provide it to him. So I am taking advantage of this opportunity today to do that.
I also wanted to correct a few misapprehensions that appear to have arisen in respect of this bill among the members of the government who have made some pretty wild-eyed observations in the course of their remarks. I think the hon. member for Ottawa West who just spoke expressed the indignation of many members on this side of the House at the government's actions in introducing this bill and in dealing with it in the way that it has. She probably also expressed the view of many of the members of the government side who are reluctant to get on their feet and say what they really think about this bill. I will proceed as best I can to point out to the government Whip and others who are here at this late hour some of the problems the Minister of Employment and Immigration brought out in the course of her introductory remarks on the motion yesterday.
The minister made a great to-do. In fact it was one of the longest speeches by a minister in this House that I have had the pleasure to witness. She seemed to have a lot of information about the historic rights of Parliament. I was delighted to hear the minister defend staunchly the
Government Orders
rights of Parliament. I have had to play that role in the House. Indeed the opposition has had to play that role now for some time against a government which seems bent on destroying the rights of Parliament.
The minister took a new tack yesterday and put herself forward as a sort of champion of parliamentary government. As reported at page 11055 of Hansard the minister said:
This House must defend its historic right to initiate and direct the financial policy of the elected government. This is not simply a theoretical exercise, but a defence of one of the key principles of responsible government. The battle for this right was won generations ago and we must protect its integrity.
That is wonderful to hear; I do not disagree with those words. The trouble is that the minister and I seem to have a profound disagreement on what it is we have to do to protect those rights.
As reported on the next page of Hansard, the minister went on to discuss British practice and spoke with longing for some kind of change in the powers of the Senate such as was introduced in 1911 in the United Kingdom to alter the powers of the House of Lords.
The minister has been a member of a government that for five years has not lifted a finger to do anything about Senate reform. The Prime Minister keeps saying that he will call a conference on Senate reform this autumn if Meech Lake passes the provinces by June. If it doesn't then he won't. I presume he is holding this out as a bit of a threat. I think most Canadians would regard that as something quite beneficial, because they realize the Senate as it currently exists provides some considerable defence for them against actions by this government which have been dictatorial in the extreme.
The minister spoke about the British practice and said how in 1911 the wings of the House of Lords were clipped. That of course has not happened in Canada.
The Prime Minister had an opportunity to make changes to the powers of the Senate as he negotiated the Meech Lake constitutional accord. I know he did not. Clearly it was not a priority. He knew, even though there was a Liberal majority in that body, the reasonableness of those senators was such that on any important issue he

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
would be able to convince them to go along with the government initiative in whole or at least in part.
I suggest the fact that the government is being very irrational in dealing with Bill C-21 is an indication of the difficulty it is having in getting that statute through the other place.
I could quote extensively from the minister's speech, but a lot of it dealt with the ins and outs of the bill. I did not want to get into that too deeply. The minister made an incredible statement on page 11062 as follows:
This government was elected in 1984 and again in 1988 largely
because Canadians understood which party could be counted on to
manage effectively.
What nonsense. That is not the reason. Hon. members opposite know perfectly well that the issue in the last campaign was free trade. It was not effective management. No Canadian in his or her right sense would have voted for a government that has managed as incompetently as this government has. It said it would cut the deficit. It has not. The deficit is still $30 billion. It said it would save Canada from financial ruin. All it has done is increased taxes, increased the amount of money the government brings in, and increased government spending at an alarming rate. That is its idea of sound financial management. I have spoken on that before and do not propose to go through it all again.
We come now to the real crux of the matter. Here we have the resolution proposed by the government. I put a question earlier to the government House leader who on April 3 in the House had the gall to stand up to argue that the amendments proposed to this bill by the other place were somehow improper.
The Speaker gave a speech on this subject on April 26. It is not quite clear to me what was the effect of the decision. It is certainly clear that the government House leader did not have the Speaker rule any of the Senate amendments out of order. The Speaker declined to make a ruling on whether or not the Senate amendments were out of order and in fact faced the government House leader who asserted they were and who now in this resolution says in fact that at least one of them is not because he approves of it. He does not have a royal recommendation to support it. If it was out of order on April 3 when he made his point, and he now says it is in order, obviously he has conceded the point. I suggest he went through a lot of bafflegab in answer to my question earlier because he really did not know what to say. He
got himself into a corner and ended up in great difficulty because he really did not understand the constitutional position in which he had placed himself in saying that the amendment is out of order. Now he is saying it is in order. He is going along with it. I congratulate him on that. I just wish he would go along with a lot more of them and, if he did, he would probably find he would have much less difficulty in getting the bill through.
That deals with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, but let us look at the government House leader because he has made some other unbelievable statements about the Constitution.
I have here a transcript of an interview he gave. He repeated some of these statements today in the House. I do not want to quote what he said because I did not write it down. I do have what he said in an interview on May 6, taped on May 4 with Pamela Wallin on the CTC news report. The minister was asked questions about his view of the role of the Senate. He made these statements which portray in my submission a profound ignorance of the Constitution of Canada.
I have urged him to spend some time in his new role reading up on this subject so he would know something more about the Constitution when he discusses it, because after all he is called upon to make comments on the role of the other place. Yet, obviously not having paid a lot of attention to this, he said:
You see, the Senate's authority comes from a clause in the Canadian Constitution that says there will be a Parliament consisting of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons. Now the Governor General has the same powers the Senate is claiming but everybody would be quite surprised, to say the least, if the Governor General said well I'm going to amend this legislation before passing it.
That is true, but had he read the Constitution Act instead of just the one clause, he would see that Section 13-and I urged him earlier today to read it-states:
The provisions of this act referring to the Governor General in Council shall be construed as referring to the Governor General acting by and with the advice of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada.
The Governor General does not go off on his or her own. The Queen or the King does not go off on his or her own, if it were a king in this particular case. The decision is made after taking advice. Everybody in Canada knows that. The Governor General cannot do anything without receiving advice on the subject except
*
May 8, 1990

on thing, and that is refuse or accept advice concerning the dissolution of the Parliament of Canada.
If the advice is refused, the Prime Minister must resign. That is just the way it is. Refusal of advice on any point results in dismissal of the cabinet.
We have had the spectacle of that happening once in 1926. But, other than that, it is just unheard of. The Governor General accepts advice from the government of the day, from the privy councillors who form the cabinet. That is the way it is. That is the way it has been in Canada for years, at least since the British North America Act was passed in 1867. So, for him to suggest that the Governor General and the Senate are similar in any way is simply beyond belief.
The minister went on. The interviewer, of course, was shocked. She said:
But that is a little bit different than a body that is-
He interrupted and said "they are both appointed", which apparently makes them the same in the view of the government House leader. He went on:
They are both appointed. In fact, Governors General are only there
for five years; Senators are there for life, for heaven's sake.
If he knew anything about the Canadian Constitution he would know that in 1965 an amendment was passed which limited senators sitting until age 75, except those appointed prior to the passage of the amendment in 1965.
Senators are not there for life unless the government House leader considers that life ends at 75. I hope, for his sake, he does not. I was hoping he would live to a ripe old age and with any luck continue to sit in this Chamber because certainly his constitutional blunders cause no end of merriment to those of us who sit on this side of the House.
I suggest that he has again blundered on with his statements as to the powers and abilities, if you like, of the Senate of Canada.
Government Orders
I could go on and argue that his views need some correction. The British North America Act, which he quoted from, has lots of sections I could read that do not reflect constitutional reality. I could turn, for example, to Section 55. Perhaps the hon. member would enjoy this:
55. Where a Bill passed by the Houses of Parliament is presented to the Governor General for the Queen's Assent, he shall declare, according to his Discretion, but subject to the Provisions of this Act and to Her Majesty's Instructions, either that he assents thereto in the Queen's Name, or that he withholds the Queen's Assent, or that he reserves the Bill for the Signification of the Queen's Pleasure.
We all know that section is no longer followed, that the Governor General invariably gives his assent to bills that are passed by this House and the other place. For the government House leader to suggest that the Senate's powers are somehow similar to those of the Governor General is simply ridiculous.
I want to turn to the questions raised by the hon. member for Kamloops who has suffered-if you want to call it that-an about face. As I said yesterday, like St. Paul on the road to Damascus at least in part, he and his party have seen the light with respect to the Senate. The NDP has recognized the true contribution that the Senate makes, and I am sorry that they are not here. I am sure they would enjoy hearing some of these things and perhaps learn some things about the Senate.
The hon. member for Kamloops explained the NDP's new position this way. It had to be one of the vaguest explanations I have ever seen. He said at page 11075 of Hansard for yesterday:
New Democrats watched intently the assault on democracy which took place last year.
Of course, so did we:
We exercised our democratic rights within our own party and voted at our December convention to change our party policy on the Senate. Whereas once we were satisfied that the Senate had to be abolished, and that was it, we are now in the process of looking at a variety of options 1o provide and promote better regional representation in the Parliament of Canada, including but not limited to, proportional representation, an elected Senate, and other options.
In other words, the New Democratic Party now has no policy on the Senate. It scrapped its abolition policy, but

May 8, 1990
Government Orders
it does not now know what it should do. That is not surprising. New Democratic Party policies change with the circumstances, just like the skin of a chameleon. In this case, we had the principle of democracy as exemplified by NDP policy, being that the Senate should be abolished.
Yesterday, we had the spectacle of the hon. member for Kamloops demanding that the Senate block this bill. In fact, he went on to say, at the same page in Hansard:
New Democrats were among those who went to the Senate and requested that it block the imposition of Bill C-21.
He was referring to New Democrats outside the House of Commons, and he made that clear. He said:
Through their labour councils, social councils, churches and women's groups, they asked the Senate to protect the unemployment insurance program that their fathers and mothers and fellow social democrats had fought so hard to establish. These ordinary New Democrats -
I presume the ones here are not ordinary:
-and ordinary Canadians generally, told the Senate of the importance of maintaining a healthy unemployment insurance program, of the need for government to play a role in training programs, of the responsibility of government toward unemployed workers.
We in this party, have said the same thing, but there is an important difference between the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party when it comes to dealing with the Senate.
The New Democratic Party said: "Use your powers as an unelected body, but use the constitutional power granted to you by the British North America Act of 1867 to block this bill." As the hon. member for Kamloops well knows, there has been no amendment made in this House similar to the British amendment of 1911 which curtailed the powers of the upper chamber. We have not done that.
The Senate has full power to change any bill that comes before it, and indeed could block this bill. The Senate has chosen not to do that, and it is not by accident that it is dominated by members of this party. We in the Liberal party do not believe that the unelected body should have the power to block the will of the democratically elected House of Commons. We have always said that. It has been our position consistently, and the position is exemplified by the actions of the Senators in the other place.

speechtext: What about the trade deal?

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
They did not reject the trade deal. What it did was say: "We will hold up, block and seek to correct the Commons in its errors. We will send the bill back with amendments." The hon. member knows that is what has happened in this case. I can see why he would flee, he does not want to face the music. Instead, the New Democratic Party has abandoned its democratic principle because it is inconvenient today. It says to the Senate: "Block this bill".
I will let you in on a secret. I know why they have said that they do not really want the Senate to block this. They say on the one hand block it, but they do not want it to happen because what they want the Senate to do is let the bill through eventually with some amendments. We are getting some more today. I see the government has softened up a bit more this time and has agreed to some of the very reasonable amendments that the Senate has proposed. Maybe if it comes back again, it will agree to more. Who knows?
What has happened is that the New Democratic Party want to be in the position where they can go to the people and say: "We urged the Senate to block this bill. We abandoned our democratic principles and we asked an unelected body to block this bill, but they did not do it".
Then they will say to the Canadian people: "Do you know why they did not do it?. Because they were Liberals and Liberals are not really in favour of protecting you by blocking this bill". That is what they will say.
They will suggest that somehow we, the opposition in this House, are somehow insincere because our colleagues in the Senate who recognize the limitations they have on their powers under the constitutional practice in Canada will not block this bill. That is what the New Democratic Party is trying to do. They are trying to have it both ways.
The trouble is in trying to get it that way they have had to abandon their democratic principles and scrap their policy of abolition of the Senate in favour of a no policy because they really have not the faintest idea of what they are going to do now.
The hon. member for Kamloops got himself into difficulty yesterday when I put these questions to him. Instead of responding in a reasonable way and admitting that their policy is folly and that they do not know what they are doing, he tried to pretend that in fact there was
May 8, 1990

a sound policy base for the actions that their party has taken. He knows as well as I do that there is no basis.
This is a chameleon-like move in an effort to fill in a vacuum that has been created because we have been defeated in this House on this matter. We have lost the vote on second and third reading after closure. The government has steamrolled the rights of parliamentarians in the course of its dealings on this bill.
What we have, I submit, is a situation where the New Democratic Party ought to be delighted that the Senate has taken the steps it has and has brought forward reasonable amendments, some of which the government has had the wisdom to accept, most of which it has not had the wisdom to accept. It should be delighted that the Senate-although they are limited amendments-have at least tried to correct the folly of the government in bringing forward this bill which is so unfair to the unemployed people of Canada.
Of course, the persons who are now employed who may subsequently become unemployed and may not
Government Orders
know it are also going to be victims under this particular piece of legislation.
I welcome the opportunity to debate these issues. I am sorry that time does not permit me to explain further the weaknesses of the New Democratic Party's position on this matter. I wish they would stay and support us in our opposition to this bill because we have indicated our anxiety to see that this bill be defeated and will continue to do so.
